During dreams, bizarre scenes you encounter can seem as tangible as reality; you feel as though you're really flying through the sky or being chased through a jungle of bright-purple trees. But in special cases, people realize they're in the midst of a dream as it's unfolding.

Called lucid dreaming, this phenomenon occurs when we suddenly regain our capacity for metacognition, or thinking about our own thoughts, in the middle of a dream. Lucid dreamers can sometimes even control the content or trajectory of their dreams. Now, researchers claim that they've found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they're awake.

In a study involving a few dozen participants, the scientists found that repeating this training twice a week for a month significantly increased how often participants experienced lucid dreaming. They say the approach could have practical applications as an intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety or post-traumatic stress disorder — but those applications are theoretical, for now.

If you could learn how to lucid dream, would you? Let us know in the poll below, and add your thoughts in the comments.

#6470. The 6 Best Electric Snowblowers Are Plenty Powerful—and Quieter Alternatives to Gas Models

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Two more reasons to go green: Battery-powered outdoor equipment is also easier to operate and store.

If you’re looking for the quickest, least labor-intensive way to dig out after a big snowstorm this winter, a snowblower is it. While it’s only fall, it’s not too early to think about getting a snow blower if you found yourself wanting one during last year’s winter storms but struggled to find a retailer that wasn’t already out of stock. Getting ahead of the game is a good idea.

Electric models are more capable than ever, and in some cases meet or exceed their gas-powered brethren in some respects. Cordless, battery-electric blowers can clear a path up to roughly 2 feet wide through as much as 20 inches of snow. They start with the push of a button, require less maintenance than gas machines, and run relatively quietly. They’re also easier to store than their gas-powered counterparts.

Ahead, we review both two-stage snow blowers and single-stage snow throwers and recommend models from Toro, Ego, Milwaukee, and more.

Our selections for this list are based on our years of testing snow blowers of all varieties. Most of these examples we’ve tested in the last few years, and others are updated versions of models we’ve tested. We are also planning for a substantial update to this guide in the coming weeks with new models.

Tony Carrick, the original author of this article, is a regular PopMech contributor and writes about everything from landscaping to home improvement. He grew up in rural Pennsylvania, where he became well-acquainted with blizzards and the backbreaking labor of digging out after them. His recommendations are based on his personal experience testing snow blowers at home, along with plenty of research to inform the picks. He compared specs for a variety of corded and cordless models, while also plowing through recommendations and feedback from dozens of customer reviews.

Electric snow blowers may not be able to match the power of their gas-powered counterparts, but this self-propelled two-stage model from Ryobi comes close. It sports four rechargeable 40-volt 6-Ah batteries, which Ryobi claims can power the snow blower for up to 45 minutes, and move the same amount of snow as a 252-cc gas-powered two-stage snow blower. It has the power to scoop up a path that’s 24 inches wide and 21 inches deep, then chuck it up to 55 feet away.

We’re also impressed with the cockpit, which allows you to control the speed of the drive wheels and the auger, change the direction of the chute, and toggle the LED headlights without missing a beat. The handlebar even heats up so your hands don’t get numb as you're working.

Our only concern is with the charger. While we like the fact that this Ryobi supports rapid charging, the charger only has two slots, which means you’ll have to go through two rounds of recharging before you’re back to full power.

If you don’t relish the idea of pushing heavy machinery through heavy snow, Snow Joe makes a lightweight single-stage snow blower that’s fairly easy to push around. At less than 38 pounds with batteries installed, the Snow Joe 24V-X2-SB18 is easy to roll out of storage, push down the driveway, and maneuver through turns.

The scraper bar clears snow right down to the pavement, and it can launch snow up to 20 feet away. On top of that, it’s very cheap—one of the most affordable cordless snow blowers we’ve found.

Unsurprisingly, that light weight and low price come with some compromises. The 18-inch-wide chute cuts a narrow path, so you’ll need to take a few extra passes to get the job done right compared to a wider machine. Meanwhile, its two 24-volt batteries offer a modest 40-minute run time.

Combine those two things, and the 24V-X2-SB18 is best reserved for smaller jobs like clearing decks, walkways, and compact driveways. If that’s what you need, though, it makes snow removal cheap and easy.

We like Ego’s battery-powered outdoor equipment because it’s among the best when it comes to power and run time—and this two-stage snow blower is no exception. With its two 56-volt, 7.5-Ah batteries and 24-inch-wide intake, the Power+ SNT2405 can clear an 8-inch layer of snow from an 18-car driveway on a single charge.

We also like the cockpit on this self-propelled machine. You can change speeds while in forward or reverse, adjust the auger speed, and change the chute direction all without having to leave the controls. It also comes equipped with four bright LED headlights, useful in the event your snow clearing efforts take you past sundown.

We also like the fact that Ego uses mostly steel construction with this machine, so you can expect it to hold up for many a winter.

Ego claims its 21-inch Power+ snow blower can throw snow up to 40 feet with a 180-degree, adjustable chute, which is pretty far for a cordless machine. In the wet sawdust test, we were able to throw 24 feet with the heavier, denser material—longer distances are certainly achievable with lighter, drier snow. It took the Power+ 4 minutes 16 seconds to clear the sawdust down to pavement in our area test.

Like most single-stage blowers, the Power+ is not self-propelled, so we needed to push it into the snow. In our dense, heavy sawdust, that took some effort to make forward progress. It’s not a bad thing, though, as it makes it easier to prevent the machine from digging in too deep and bogging down. In very wet or ice-packed snow, we expect you’ll have to put in a similar effort.

The Power+ has a variable-speed auger, so we were able to adjust speed for the conditions and conserve battery when less power was needed. There isn’t too much to worry about in the battery department, since it comes with two 5-Ah batteries, enough to clear 8 inches of snow on a 12-car driveway—that’s six cars long by two cars wide.

The Power+ comes with a dual-port charger, so the two batteries can be charged simultaneously to get you ready for the next round faster. Ego rounds things out with front-mounted LEDs for low-light and dark conditions, plus an easy-folding handle for stowing the unit when not in use.

The 60-volt 26-inch Power Max e26 is one of the models we tested in November 2025, and it’s among the burliest two-stage cordless snow blowers we’ve used. It is built virtually the same as a gas model, except with an electric motor and two batteries. That includes the frame, drive system, auger, and auger housing.

Since it’s built the same, we can confirm it performs the same—so it could easily replace a similar gas model. No caveats here; the Power Max e26 isn’t a compromise in any significant way that we could determine. It comes with two batteries and a (claimed) runtime up to 70 minutes—enough to clear a driveway 30 car spaces long.

Operating the Power Max e26 was a pleasant experience, if you can call snow blowing pleasant. It has effective heated hand grips, and an axle with a differential that allows you to turn quickly, on a dime—no having to muscle it around.

The e26 easily handled our testing with wet sawdust, throwing it far enough to cross an average driveway—even when making a full 26-inch-wide pass. If you’ve questioned whether a cordless snow blower could ever be as good as a gas machine, the e26 answers that affirmatively.

Milwaukee’s M18 single-stage snow blower is the second machine we tested in November 2025, and it also impressed us. It's noticeably heavier than many other similar cordless models, which seems to be due to its metal frame. At 90 pounds, it isn’t heavy, at least in comparison to two-stage machines, but the weight is an advantage, helping prevent the blower from bouncing around or riding up when encountering denser, crusty snow.

We tested this snow blower with wet sawdust, which always presents a little bit of a challenge with single-stage snow blowers, as they have to lift the snow and eject it in one operation. Milwaukee’s M18 blower did this well enough in testing—and if it can throw wet sawdust, it will really throw the snow.

To facilitate ejecting snow, the M18’s chute is wider than that of most other models. This eliminates potential bottlenecks and ultimately clogs, where the snow passes from the blower body into the chute. Milwaukee's single auger is edged with a rubber paddle that both sweeps the pavement clean and pulls the machine forward. It does this well enough that, in some instances, we had to hold it back a little in testing.

The chute has a remote adjustment—you can crank a knob just below the handlebar to change the direction of the chute, allowing you to put snow where it needs to go. However, ejection elevation is manually adjusted at the top of the chute—but this isn't something you typically need to adjust as often.

Milwaukee claims the M18 blower can clear up to 11 parking places, or 500 feet of sidewalk on the two included 12.0-Ah batteries. But with two extra battery ports, you can double the runtime by adding another pair of batteries. We’ll be testing this more as we have snow available.

There are two types of snow blowers for homeowners, based on the number of “stages” in the mechanical process they use to collect and distribute snow.

Single-stage snow blowers have an auger that pulls the snow into a large intake at the front of the snow blower, and propels it out of a chute mounted to the top of the machine. Single-stage blowers, also frequently referred to as “snow throwers,” are small, lightweight and easy to maneuver, making them ideal for clearing light snowfall and smaller driveways and walks.

Dual-stage snow blowers, as the name suggests, have a two-stage process for collecting and expelling snow. Like single-stage models, they have an auger that pulls snow into the intake. The dual-stage snow blower follows up by pushing the snow into an impeller that ejects it out through the chute.

The one-two punch of auger and impeller allows a two-stage snow blower to remove more snow quicker, and throw it a longer distance. That makes them perfect for large driveways. That said, they are larger and heavier than single-stage machines, so they may not be able to maneuver around narrow walking paths as easily.

The width and depth of a snow blower’s intake determine how much snow it can move with each pass, and thus, how long it takes you to get the job done. Most single-stage electric snow blowers have a clearing width of around 20 inches and a clearing depth of around 8 inches. That’s good for carving out walks and medium-sized areas. Some heavy-duty two-stage electric snow blowers can remove a 24-inch-wide and 20-inch-deep swath of snow, which will make quick work of a large driveway.

Throwing distance refers to how far a snow blower can launch snow out of the chute. This gives you a sense of how to plan when and how you’ll dispose of the snow in your path. The average single-stage snow blower typically has a short throwing distance—around 25 feet. Unsurprisingly, a two-stage snow blower can send its snow as far as 50 feet.

Snow blowers typically have a throttle that allows you to change their mechanical speed, which will adjust how far it throws your snow. There are also controls that allow you to rotate the chute to change the direction of the flow of snow. If you can map out your snow-blowing route, check and make sure your snow blower throws the snow far enough to keep it out of your way until it melts.

Most electric snow blowers receive power from multiple large rechargeable batteries, which allow them to produce nearly as much power as a gas snow blower. No battery supplies uninterrupted power for as long as a tank of gas, though: On average, you should expect a battery-powered snow blower to run for about 30 to 45 minutes on a single charge. You can extend that time if you have multiple batteries, but the low run time still caps how much ground they can cover.

Though we largely consider them to be obsolete, some manufacturers also still produce corded electric snow blowers, which plug into a standard electrical outlet. They’re often cheaper than battery-powered models and run as long as you need them to. However, having a power cord substantially reduces their range: You will likely need to purchase an extension cord to extend its reach slightly beyond the length of the area you need to clear. No matter how much slack you have, though, the cable makes the whole process a little more awkward.

“Cordless snow blowers are easier, better, and safer to use,” says Popular Mechanics Test Editor Brad Ford. “Corded is old, out-of-date tech in most cases.”

They’re also limited to smaller, 15-amp motors that run on the power an outlet can provide. That usually translates to narrower clearing widths, shallower clearing depths, and shorter throw distances. Unless you have a very tight budget, we highly recommend going with a battery-powered electric snow blower rather than a corded one.

The most important thing you can do to keep your electric snow blower running season after season is to simply make sure that you store your charger and batteries indoors when you aren’t charging or using them. Lithium cells aren't able to hold the same amount of charge when the temperature drops below freezing. By storing and charging those batteries indoors, you’ll get the most run time out of them.

If you use a corded snow blower, you shouldn’t plug it into any old extension cord. These machines draw a lot of power, and not every cord can handle it. Using the wrong one can create a fire hazard or damage your snow blower. Make sure to check your snow blower’s specs before buying an extension cord to pair with it, so you can be sure it can handle its amperage.

Most corded electric snow blowers have a 12-amp rating, in which case you’ll want a 12-gauge extension cord that can provide at least 12 amps of power. You’ll also want to make sure it’s long enough for you to reach the far end of whatever walkway or road you plan to clear, preferably with some slack to spare for maneuverability. We recommend starting with 100 feet and scaling up based on your property.

Regardless, it would be wise to buy an extension cord to match the specs you need for your snow blower, rather than using one that you happen to have lying around.

With advancements in battery technology, there are now powerful two-stage cordless snow blowers capable of clearing deeper, heavier snow.

That said, the most powerful electric snow blowers still don’t match the snow-moving capabilities of the largest gas-powered snow blowers on the market. The most powerful electric snow blowers work best at maximum depths of about a foot, while some gas-powered models can clear snow up to 2 feet deep.

Tony Carrick is a full-time freelance writer who specializes in technology, home improvement, DIY, home security, and outdoor recreation. He’s tested and written about everything from home security systems to power tools to gas grills. His product guides, how-to articles, and feature stories can be found in such publications as Bob Vila, Angi, U.S. News and World Report, Field & Stream, Futurism, and Switchful. #6469. The Ice Giants' Magnetic Fields are Very Strange Compared to Earth's

Most planets appear to have magnetic fields, even if they're only weak, remnant fields. Earth has a strong field generated by its internal geodynamo. The other rocky planets have magnetic fields of varying strengths, with the possible exception of Venus. The outer gas planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, all have strong dynamos.

But the magnetic fields generated by the ice giants Uranus and Neptune have some strange properties.

Earth's molten core and internal convection generate its magnetic fields. But the ice giants' magnetic fields are likely generated by fluids that are electrically conductive. These are water, ammonia, and methane ices under extreme pressure and temperatures that alter them and turn them into ionic and superionic phases. Not only is their electrical conductivity at play, but so is convection and the planets' rotations.

But beyond what generates them, they also have other differences. Earth's magnetic field has well-defined north and south poles that drift a little over time, and even flip every couple of hundred thousand years or so. But Voyager 2 showed us how different Uranus and Neptune are. Their fields are in disarray compared to Earth's. They're tilted and multi-peaked.

Uranus' magnetic field doesn't originate in its center, and is tilted almost 60 degrees from its axis of rotation. It's overall geometry is strange, and the magnetic field across its surface is asymmetrical in strength.

Neptune's magnetic field is similarly strange, but weaker. Like Uranus' it's tilted from its rotational axis, by about 47 degrees. It's also offset from the planet's physical center like Uranus'.

The most critical difference between the magnetic fields of Earth and those of Uranus and Neptune is that the fields around the ice giants experience shorter-term variability. In short, they're a weird mess.

While planetary scientists know that these fields are generated inside the planets, they've had to make some guesses as to why they're so strange. New research in Nature Communications Physics has made some progress understanding the pair of ice giants and their strange magnetic fields. It's titled "Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune," and the lead author is Chi Yan. Yan is a research associate at the University of Texax Jackson School of Geosciences.

"Uranus and Neptune exhibit magnetic fields that are non-dipolar and non-axisymmetric, unlike those of any other known planet," the researchers write. "These fields are generated by fluid motions in electrically conducting planetary interiors via dynamo action, offering a window into otherwise inaccessible deep processes."

As we often say at Universe Today, understanding the oddballs and outliers in a group of objects sheds light on how processes operate across the broader group they're a part of. This is true of the ice giants and their magnetic fields. "Understanding why Uranus and Neptune have such unusual magnetic fields provides critical insight into dynamo processes across planets and stars," the authors explain.

This work is based on modelled dynamos that are controlled by interior composition and temperature. They assumed that electrical conductivity increases with depth. The authors say they "produce large-scale magnetic features consistent with the observed fields of Uranus and Neptune..."

This schematic shows the different interior layouts used in the models. a through c show radially variable electrical conductivity profiles for dynamo models with convective shell geometries. d through f show the associated shell geometry for each of a through c. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

âDeep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high,â lead author Yan said in a press release. âUnder these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.â

Voyager 2 gave us our only good close-up look at Uranus and Neptune. It likely caught those fields in a snapshot in time, and the model shows both planets' magnetic fields could shift and change markedly in only decades. The fields are most likely configured much differently than when Voyager 2 visited. This is much different than on Earth, where the magnetic north pole drifts between about 5 and 60 km per year, or about one degree every few decades.

"These non-dipolar dynamos exhibit substantial temporal variation, although the rate fluctuates and can be transiently slow," the authors write. They explain that changes in both intensity and orientation are a possibility in the decades since Voyager 2 flew past Uranus and Neptune, "though the extent of any such variation remains poorly constrained observationally as each planet has been measured in situ only once."

âEarthâs magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years,â said Yan. âOur models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.â

This figure compares observations of Uranus' and Neptune's surface magnetic fields with the fields from models. The figure "demonstrates that the most Uranus-like snapshot from Model 6 (panel c) and the most Neptune-like snapshot from Model 11 (panel d) can change substantially on decadal timescales, with their close morphological resemblance to the respective observed fields (panels a and b) deteriorating markedly after 32 years (panels e and f)," the authors explain. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

"We demonstrate that dynamo models incorporating an electrical conductivity that increases with depth can promote non-dipolar, non-axisymmetric magnetic fields," the authors write, including the M1 peak observed at Uranus and Neptune.

The M1 peak is an important, maybe the most important part, of Voyager 2's magnetic field observations. M=1 represents the lop-sided parts of a magnetic field. On Earth and other planets like Jupiter and Saturn, the magnetic field's power is dominated by symmetric or M=0 components. So for those planets, the M-1 components are at least an order of magnitude weaker than their M-0 components.

But that's not true on Uranus and Neptune. They show a stark contrast. They both have a very strong M-1 peak, the part that represents asymmetric fields. This means that they have dipoles, quadrupoles, and octupoles that are messy and skewed from the axis of rotation.

"Despite current observational and computational limitations, our results indicate that ice-giant-like dynamos can, in some intervals, undergo substantial magnetic field variations on decadal timescales that, if confirmed by future in situ or auroral measurements, could have significant impacts on the surrounding planetary magnetospheres," the authors write.

The JWST has observed the ice giant aurorae and the charged particles involved. These particles respond to the magnetic fields, and those observations could confirm if the magnetic fields have indeed shifted since Voyager 2 visited. Researchers are still working on those observations.

The image on the left is an enhanced-color image of Neptune from NASAâs Hubble Space Telescope. On the right, that image is combined with data from NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope. The cyan splotches are auroral activity captured with the JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec). Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Heidi Hammel (AURA), Henrik Melin (Northumbria University), Leigh Fletcher (University of Leicester), Stefanie Milam (NASA-GSFC)

âWe are busy working on whatâs contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an important stepping stone,â said Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign.

The researchers will combine the JWST data with their models and data from Voyager 2 and take their results as far as they can to try to determine the state of the magnetic fields today. But they're up against some limitations, limitations that can only be lifted by another mission to the ice giants.

There are no firm plans for a mission to the ice giants, but there are concepts. One is NASA's Uranus Orbiter & Probe that would study the planet and its moons, and even send a probe into Uranus' atmosphere. The Neptune Odyssey is another NASA concept. It would also consist of an orbiter and an atmospheric probe. The science community has recognized the importance of these missions, but they're just concepts at this point.

This research may extend to the issue of habitability, though probably only tangentially. Uranus' four major moons could all potentially have subsurface oceans under icy covers, though this is far from confirmed. If they do, then Uranus' magnetic field and related radiation belts could affect these bodies of water, their longevity, and their potential habitability.

#6468. Cancer Immunotherapy Has a Dangerous Side Effect. Scientists May Have Found a Way To Stop It

Cancer immunotherapy could become safer by stabilizing the cells that keep immune responses under control, an approach that reversed treatment-related inflammation in mice.

Some cancer patients have to stop immunotherapy when their immune system starts attacking healthy tissue. These reactions can occur with drugs called immune checkpoint inhibitors, which help immune cells known as T cells fight cancer by releasing the brakes that normally restrain them.

Depending on the type of checkpoint inhibitor, 20% to 40% of patients experience these immune-related adverse events. Up to 25% experience severe reactions that result in hospitalization and an end to treatment. There are no U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved treatments for these side effects.

“Immune-related adverse events are a huge problem and can greatly impact quality of life for patients. In many cases, it impacts their ability to stay on immunotherapy or benefit from treatment,” said Abigail Overacre-Delgoffe, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Department of Immunology at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and a member of the Tumor Microenvironment Center at UPMC Hillman Cancer Center.

Overacre-Delgoffe is the senior author of a study published October 22, 2026, in Cell that identifies unstable immune cells as a potential driver of this inflammation. Her team reversed inflammation in mice by blocking a protein in those cells and found that diet and the gut microbiome, the community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, influenced the severity of the animals’ reactions.

Studying these side effects has been difficult because they vary considerably among patients. Animal models have also struggled to reproduce the complexity of immune-related inflammation in humans.

“Most existing mouse models relied on genetically modified mice or experimental conditions that didn’t really capture the variability we see in patients,” said lead author Dipyaman Patra, Ph.D., a postdoctoral associate in Overacre-Delgoffe’s lab. “This got us thinking about whether common lifestyle factors, particularly diet and the gut microbiome, could influence the host immune system even before immunotherapy begins.”

Overacre-Delgoffe’s earlier work had shown that diet and gut microbes can influence cancer patient outcomes and responses to immunotherapy. To investigate their role in treatment side effects, her team fed mice a diet designed to resemble a Western-style human diet, low in fiber and high in fat and processed carbohydrates. The animals began eating it two weeks before checkpoint inhibitor therapy and continued during treatment.

The mice became susceptible to immune-related adverse events and developed immune and microbiome changes resembling many of those seen in affected patients. This gave the researchers a way to test how gut microbes contributed to the inflammation.

Transferring fecal microbes from mice eating the Western-style diet into mice eating a regular, high-fiber diet caused gut inflammation in the recipients. Transfers could also reduce inflammation. Male mice were less susceptible to severe adverse events, and transferring their fecal microbes into female mice reduced the severity of inflammation in the females.

The team also transferred fecal microbes from patients consuming a Western-style diet into germ-free mice, which are raised without microorganisms. Those recipients developed more severe immune-related adverse events. Together, the transfer experiments provided evidence that the microbiome could influence the severity of these reactions in mice.

Within the immune system, the researchers identified a problem involving regulatory T cells. These cells normally suppress excessive immune responses, but stress can make them unstable, a condition called regulatory T cell fragility. Mice eating the Western-style diet showed signs of this fragility during immunotherapy. The researchers found the same instability in regulatory T cells collected from patients with severe immune-related adverse events, but not in cells from patients without the side effect.

Blocking an immune-signaling protein specifically on regulatory T cells restored their stability in mice and reversed inflammation. Switching the animals to a high-fiber diet or giving them supplements containing metabolites, substances produced through metabolism, also stabilized the cells. Restoring stability significantly reduced the severity of adverse events, supporting the interpretation that regulatory T cell fragility is a major underlying cause in this model.

“We were able to generate the first of its kind preclinical mouse model of adverse events that didn’t require full gene knockouts,” said Overacre-Delgoffe. “By combining this novel preclinical model alongside patient data, we were able to identify a very new mechanism of adverse events that hopefully will result in new targeted therapies, allowing more cancer patients to stay on treatment and out of the hospital.”

The model will give researchers a platform to investigate why some patients develop severe reactions and to identify biological markers that might predict susceptibility. Future work will explore drug targets in specific tissues that could limit or eliminate these side effects without disrupting immunotherapy. Metabolite supplementation is another potential approach to reducing susceptibility without interfering with the microbiome, although its promise here comes from experiments in mice.

“We now have some potential targets that we’re going after that seem to limit immune-related adverse events without negatively impacting immunotherapy, which would be the first of its kind and is quite exciting” Overacre-Delgoffe said.

Reference: “Lifestyle-induced regulatory T cell fragility primes adverse events after immune checkpoint blockade” by Dipyaman Patra, Katelyn Wolfgang, Chenxian Ye, Lora Rigatti, Kelsey Ertwine, Kristin M. Morder, Jessica Jana, Ishita Baral, Drew Hurd, Kaitlin Bossong, Steven Mullett, Yingtong Dou, Stacy Gelhaus, Dario A.A. Vignali, Diwakar Davar, Anthony R. Cillo, Greg M. Delgoffe and Abigail E. Overacre-Delgoffe, 22 October 2026, Cell. DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.055

Old STAR Award (CRI3447), Sy Holzer Endowed Immunotherapy Fund, The Pittsburgh Foundation (MR2023-134140), National Institute of Allergy & Infectious Diseases (R01AI171483, R01AI166598), National Cancer Institute (P30CA047904, R01CA277473, P50CA121973, P50CA097190), and UPMC Hillman Cancer Center Skin Cancer and Head and Neck Cancer SPOREs.

A very interesting study. Nothing in medicine is adverse-effect-free!! However, if this study only involves changing the gut environment and a high-fibre diet, which everyone should be on anyway, why not just tell people on cancer immunotherapy to abide by the regimen? I also understand that the effect needs to be tested in animals, but the poor mice have to have cancer and then be treated with the new hypothesis.

#6467. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

#6466. More Than a Billion Years of Earth’s History Is Missing – Scientists May Finally Know Why

Earth’s rocks are missing more than a billion years of history in some places, and the slow rise and fall of continents may explain how those chapters disappeared.

A study led by University of Wollongong (UOW) PhD candidate Santosh Dhungana suggests that the slow rise and fall of continents helped create the Great Unconformity, a vast gap in Earth’s geological record. Published in Nature, the research links this missing history to currents of hot rock in the mantle that moved continents vertically over hundreds of millions of years.

Normally, rock layers preserve a sequence of events, with younger deposits accumulating above older ones. At the Great Unconformity, that sequence jumps: sedimentary rocks from around the beginning of the Cambrian period, roughly 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite more than a billion years old.

“Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth’s story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren’t lost by chance,” Dhungana said.

The Grand Canyon exposes one of the most striking examples of this geological gap. It lies within what was once the ancient continent Laurentia (modern North America). Similar boundaries appear in Europe, Australia, Africa, and Asia, although the missing intervals vary from about 200 million years to well over a billion.

Explaining the Great Unconformity requires accounting for both the removal of rock and the survival of the eroded surface beneath younger deposits. Dhungana said that although scientists had offered several explanations, those ideas had not been thoroughly tested against Earth’s behavior over time.

To investigate, he and his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, modeled mantle convection across hundreds of millions of years. The mantle consists of hot, solid rock that flows very slowly. Its currents can gently lift enormous stretches of land or allow them to sink.

The models indicated that mantle currents raised the ancient continental cores of Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe), and North China during the Neoproterozoic Era, from about one billion to 540 million years ago. This prolonged uplift would have exposed rock to erosion. The era was followed by the Cambrian period, when animal life diversified dramatically.

The next stage helped preserve what erosion had left behind. During the Phanerozoic eon, which spans the past 540 million years, the continental cores gradually sank. Seas spread across their worn surfaces, and accumulating sediment buried the boundary between the ancient rocks and the younger geological record.

The modeled pattern matched the geography of the evidence. North America, northern Europe, and North China, where the Great Unconformity is especially well preserved and documented, all showed the prolonged rise followed by sinking that the researchers proposed.

“Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface,” Associate Professor Flament said.

“Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed, but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.”

Reference: “The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity” by Santosh Dhungana, and Nicolas Flament, 4 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11156-5

This study was funded by the Australian Research Council.

#6465. Astrophysicists Want to Forecast When a Black Hole Launches Its Jets

Black holes are not just objects. Some astrophysicists prefer to call them locations. From this vantage point, they're locations where the Universe's laws of physics are pushed to their extreme limits.

Black holes are gravitational gluttons that draw everything in their vicinity towards them. When another star strays too close, the black hole can strip its gas away. The gas doesn't necessarily disappear over the event horizon and leave our observable Universe. It first gathers in a rapidly rotating accretion disk, where its temperature is raised to extreme levels. Some of this superheated material is ejected in a pair of collimated jets from the black hole's axis of rotation.

These jets are streams of plasma and particles that can reach relativistic speeds. They can have an enormous reach; the largest ones come from supermassive black holes and can extend for millions of parsecs into space. Though astrophysicists have witnessed many of these jets, their exact causes remain uncertain. The extreme gravity, magnetic fields, and temperatures around black holes is all a part of it.

Astrophysical jets shape their surroundings by heating star forming gas and moving it around on a massive scale. Stars form from cool gas, and the energy from jets works directly against that. The jets can also inflate bubbles where gas is too diffuse to collapse and form stars.

This JWST NIRCam image shows the jets coming from Messier 87, one of the most massive galaxies in the local Universe. These jets aren't from an x-ray binary, they're from its central SMBH that has billions of solar masses. It's an example of extreme astrophysical jets and an indicator of the extreme physics at black holes. Image Credit: Jan RÃ¶der, Maciek Wielgus et al., Astronomy & Astrophysics (2025)

Astrophysicists want to be able to predict when these jets are triggered so they can quickly gather follow-up observations, and new research in The Astrophysical Journal has made some progress. It's titled "Jet Forecast: Timing of Discrete Jet Ejections of Stellar-mass Black Holes Anticipated via X-Ray Properties," and the authors are Toshihiro Kawaguchi and Kazutaka Yamaoka. Kawaguchi is from the Graduate School of Science and Engineering at the University of Toyama, and Yamaoka is from the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University.

The pair of researchers have been working on this problem for a while. In a 2025 study, they examined an x-ray binary consisting of a black hole and a donor star and found a link between the parameters of the inner accretion disk and jet activity. That research suggested that as the accretion disk's inner edge shrank towards its innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO), the black hole launched its jets. "This fact suggests that the jet materials originate from accreting matter from the innermost part of the disk," the authors wrote.

That was progress, but in that paper the researchers pointed out that more observations were needed. "Both X-ray spectral and timing observations are very important to understand the accretion disk states which can change very rapidly. Dense, simultaneous coverage with radio observations are also crucial to understand diskâjet interactions," the authors wrote in the conclusion to their 2025 paper.

This illustration is representative of XTE J1859+226, the system the authors studied in their 2025 paper. It shows a black hole not only drawing material away from the donor star, but also stretching the star into a distorted shape. Image Credit: J. M. Corral-Santana/Corral-Santana et al. 2011 MNRAS

Their 2025 paper was based on observations of a single black hole x-ray binary gathered during an outburst in 1999â2000. This work is based on observations of four black hole binary systems: one from the 2025 paper and three new ones.

There seem to be changes in an x-ray binary's (XRB) x-ray emissions prior to jets being launched. The spectrum is altered, and variability decreases. Astrophysicists have interpreted these changes as a signal that jets are about to be emitted. But the signals haven't been clear and reliable enough, so astrophysicists haven't been able to use them to time their follow-up observations. The researchers' previous work showed that as an accretion disk's inner edge shrank down to its ISCO, jets were launched. This could be the reliable signal astrophysicists are searching for.

This work expands their observations to more XRBs to see if this holds true. The researchers hope to develop a forecasting model for XRB jet launching so that more complete observations can be obtained.

The results show that the rapidly decreasing radius of the inner disk, called Rin, combined with a decrease in x-ray emission variability (indicated by rms), are a reliable predictor of jet launching. "All the four sources turned out to show the precursors of jet ejections (drops in Rin and rms) 1â10 days before radio activities," the authors write.

This artistâs depiction of a jet ejection shows how the jet from the black hole turns on when the inner radius of the accretion disk shrinks down to the ISCO fast enough. Image Credit: Professor Toshihiro Kawaguchi from University of Toyama, Japan and Dr. Kazutaka Yamaoka from Nagoya University, Japan.

They also found that there are no reliably detected increases in the amount of mass accreted prior to the launching of jets. "They show no huge jumps in M prior to each jet ejection," the researchers explain.

In at least one of the XRBs, that rate actually decayed in the 30 days leading up to jet launching. "We examined the time evolution of the accretion rate M of XTE J1859. It turned out to be exponentially decaying during the outburst (with an e-folding timescale of â¼30 days), and shows no huge jumps around the jet ejections," they write.

But XTE J1859 did show a tantalizing hint of enhancement. "There is a hint of â¼20% enhancement in M just before the jet productions," the authors write.

But that's just a hint, and better observations are needed to support it. "Such fine structures in the time evolution of M will be examined by the better data via the âjet forecastâ in the future," the researchers write.

Another notable finding concerns the Eddington limit. It's a theoretical threshold balanced between the inward force of gravity and the outward force of radiation. In two of the four systems, jets formed below this threshold. Some models of jet ejection say that super-Eddington accretion beyond this limit is necessary to launch jets, but these results say otherwise.

âMonitoring of Rin seems to be suitable for predicting the timing of jet ejections,â said Prof. Kawaguchi. âThe development of a âjet forecastâ would enable us to concentrate observing facilities on the expected timing of jet ejections, thereby accelerating our understanding of jet physics.â

Their jet forecasting model would be based on shrinking Rin and X-ray variability, and when both are detected, alerts would be sent out to other telescopes for more complete observations. Those observation would hopefully reveal some more of the extreme physics that dominate and define black holes.

"When both Rin and rms continuously decrease and when Rin is about to reach the ISCO, alerts can be circulated as a âjet forecastâ for triggering ToO (Target of Opportunity) observations," the authors write.

This is more than just purely academic. Earth has been subjected to bombardment by high-energy particles throughout its history. The Earth's protective magnetic shield deflects most of them, but some get through and trigger showers of secondary particles. Convincing evidence is thin, but some researchers still consider them a factor in the course of life on Earth.

âJet ejections in the Universe produce high-energy photons and particles, such as neutrinos, and such cosmic rays have long influenced the evolution of living creatures on Earth, including human beings,â concluded Prof. Kawaguchi.

#6464. Scientists Solved the Mystery of Why Some People Shiver in the Cold While Others Wear Shorts

Experiments in mice suggest that testosterone and a molecular cold sensor shape who reaches for the parka.

Shuffling outside in three layers and a parka to pick up mail or take out the trash on a winter afternoon, you notice your neighbor is running the same errand in a sweatshirt and shorts. Just the sight of this gives you the chills, as if you weren’t shivering already. Could there be some freakish biological reason that, unlike your neighbor, you can hardly even imagine yourself in something that isn’t heavyweight and lined with fleece when the sky is threatening snow?

Like with plenty of other quirks of our daily lived experiences, the answer to that question is yes.

Your tolerance of the heat or the cold may actually be determined at a molecular level. Researchers Peter McNaughton and Bruno Vilar of Wolfson Sensory, Pain and Regeneration Centre at King’s College London exposed mice to different temperatures and saw that female mice preferred higher temperatures than males. The mice were given a choice of two heated metal plates, and the females scurried to the warmer plate at 100.4°F (38°C) while males would crawl towards the cooler control plate kept at 91.4°F (33°C). It was only when the researchers began to alter certain genetic mechanisms that the mice changed their preferences.

“Human females have a lower surface temperature and a higher central temperature than males and prefer a higher ambient temperature,” McNaughton and Vilar said in a study recently published in The Journal of Physiology. “Although the comfort temperature varies significantly among species, a sex difference in thermal preference is consistent in most bird species and in mammals such as mice.”

The answer lies in ion channels, tiny pores in cell membranes that let electrically charged particles called ions flow in and out. Two of them, TRPM2 and TRPM8, work as temperature sensors. Among other functions, TRPM2 regulates adaptations related to heat, while TRPM8 is activated by cold. Mice were allowed to feel out the heated plates for half an hour and usually showed a final preference halfway through the time they were given. There was no significant difference between male and female mice when they had to choose between the control plate and one at a cooler temperature of either 82.4°F (28°C) or 73.4°F (23°C). Both the male and female mice preferred the control plate to anything cooler. But then things began to get heated.

Distinct preferences began to appear when the mice had the opportunity to decide between the control plate and a warmer alternative. Most females began shifting over to the warm plate and spent more time there, while males, whose preferred ambient temperature is known to be about the same as that of the control plate, apparently found that more tolerable. Upping the temperature of one plate to 109.4°F (43°C) had the same effect. The biological females preferred an average temperature of 96.8°F (36°C) while males’ average preferred temp was 89.42°F (31.9°C). Core body temperature doesn’t explain the difference. Male and female mice have the same core temperature, but the females still went looking for more heat.

Genetic experiments helped show what drives the difference. When researchers deleted TRPM2 in male mice, the males suddenly moved toward the warmer plate, just as the females did. Deleting TRPM2 in females barely changed anything. TRPM8 played a much more significant role. When it was blocked with an injection or deleted entirely, both female and male mice stopped avoiding the cold and readily moved onto the cooler plate. This shows that TRPM8 is essential for sensing cold. A third channel, TRPV1, turned out to matter only for detecting intense heat.

Hormones explain part of the difference, and testosterone seems to be the main one. Lowering testosterone in male mice shifted them toward the females’ preference for warmth, and giving females extra testosterone made them more averse to heat. Estradiol and progesterone, the main female sex hormones, had no effect. Even so, testosterone didn’t account for the whole gap between the sexes.

“The simplest explanation of these observations is that TRPM2 and TRPM8 are expressed in different peripheral thermally sensitive nerve terminals,” the researchers said, “where they drive the generation of action potentials that convey thermal sensation to the [central nervous system].”

This tiny inkwell contains an alphabetic inscription in ancient Etruscan, a language that has never been fully decoded.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The chicken-shaped, black-glazed vase has an abecedarium ‪—‬ an inscription with the 26 letters of the Etruscan alphabet in order.

What it is: A bird-shaped ceramic inkwell

This small terra-cotta vase, which is shaped like a cockerel or young male chicken with human feet, was discovered in central Italy and was made by the ancient Etruscans. The potter inscribed the Etruscan alphabet on the body of the chicken, giving modern researchers clues to a language that has never been fully deciphered.

The vase stands just over 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. The dark-black ceramic, known as bucchero, was made through a unique firing method that prevented the kiln from getting enough oxygen, which caused the clay to absorb carbon. Bucchero is considered the trademark Etruscan ceramic, and it was produced from the seventh to the fourth centuries B.C. by this pre-Roman society. It is unclear where the cockerel vase was originally found, but it may have been discovered in a grave in one of the many cemeteries that surround Viterbo, which was originally an Etruscan town about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northwest of modern-day Rome.

According to The Met, the vase may have been a portable inkwell used by an ancient Etruscan who was learning how to write. The cockerel's head was the stopper, and it was loosely attached to the body by a cord through a set of loops. The inscription on the body of the vase is known as an abecedarium ‪—‬ the sequential list of letters in an alphabet.

The Etruscan alphabet is well known, since it was adopted from a regional version of the Greek alphabet in the early eighth century B.C. There were 26 letters in the Etruscan alphabet, but one of them in this abecedarium is incorrect. A close look at the end of the alphabet shows that someone inscribed an S twice; the second one should look more like an X, according to The Met.

The terracotta cockerel vase was one of several ancient Etruscan artifacts that helped experts partially decode the mysterious ancient language, as it preserved the order of the letters in the early alphabet, archaeologist Gisela Richter wrote in a 1930 catalog of The Met's classical artifacts.

Thanks to the adoption of the Greek alphabet, it's possible to fully sound out the Etruscan language. But although more than 10,000 Etruscan inscriptions have been found, the language is still only partially understood because those inscriptions are short and any lengthy Etruscan literature that once existed has been lost.

#6462. This $10,000-a-Pound Spice Could Help Save Colorado Farmers

Beneath Denver’s solar panels, a spice nicknamed “red gold” is yielding a promising harvest that could help Colorado farmers earn more with less water.

At Colorado State University Spur, horticulture graduate student Reece Bailey is investigating whether saffron could become a profitable addition to the state’s farms. His experiments in the campus’s urban gardens and green roof research areas are testing how the crop handles Colorado’s climate, how much water it needs, and whether growing it beneath solar panels improves production.

The appeal starts with its extraordinary value. A pound of saffron typically costs between $600 and $5,000, with some varieties reaching $10,000. Vanilla, the second most expensive spice, sells for roughly $90 to $225 a pound. Those prices caught Bailey’s attention, but the research must establish whether the potential earnings justify the work.

Colorado may seem an unlikely home for a spice closely associated with the Middle East. Yet Iran, which produces roughly 85% of the world’s saffron, has mountainous, semiarid conditions that resemble parts of the state. Bailey sees that overlap as a reason to investigate whether “red gold” could find a foothold on Colorado’s high plains.

The crop also offers an unusual combination of low water demand and late production. Saffron typically blooms in November, potentially bringing farmers income after other harvests have ended. Under suitable conditions, Bailey said, it could provide that additional crop without requiring extra irrigation.

“One thing that’s always been interesting to me is new ideas and novel ways of integrating crops into our environments,” said Bailey, who grew up in Aurora and has worked on Spur’s green roof for three years.

The world’s most expensive spice comes from a remarkably small harvest: the three slender red stigmas inside each purple saffron flower. Collecting enough to produce a pound of dried spice requires roughly 75,000 flowers.

That harvest is painstaking. Flowers open for only a few hours each morning, and workers carefully extract the stigmas, often with tweezers. The amount of hand labor helps explain both saffron’s price and the challenge of turning it into a profitable crop.

“It’s certainly not the easiest crop to grow or the easiest crop to work with, but the investment can be well worth it,” Bailey said.

The Colorado Department of Agriculture has committed $80,000 through its Specialty Crop Block Grant Program to investigate that possibility, particularly as a source of supplemental income late in the season and during dry years.

“For a lot of farmers, the price for their goods isn’t keeping up with the price of inputs, so what we’re really trying to do is find new crops that will work with Colorado’s climate and for our producers’ bottom line,” said Sam Hahn, the department’s next generation and specialty crops program manager. “Saffron has a high labor input, but it could really be a boon for our farmers.”

Successfully growing the flowers would answer only part of the business question. Farmers would still need to assess startup costs, bulb suppliers, equipment, labor availability, and buyers. A valuable spice does not automatically translate into a profitable harvest.

Its labor demands could nevertheless create another benefit. Hahn said the November bloom might provide agricultural jobs during a period when many farmworkers are typically unemployed, while helping farms adapt to a changing climate.

“It’s so important that we experiment with these high-value crops to see if it can supplement the market in our state and keep us competitive,” Hahn said.

Some of the most promising results are emerging 75 feet (23 meters) above the ground. Bailey’s plots occupy the roofs of two CSU Spur buildings, with Denver’s skyline and the Rocky Mountains in view. One grows among native Colorado plants, including sunflowers. Another sits beneath solar panels in an agrivoltaic system, where the same space supports crops and electricity production.

“I’m always curious about how different plants evolve and how they adapt to green roofs, and lately, I’ve come to realize that saffron is almost the ideal plant for these environments,” said Jennifer Bousselot, Bailey’s faculty adviser and an associate professor of horticulture and landscape architecture at CSU.

Spur’s rooftop gardens have carefully selected soil characteristics and are designed to use water efficiently. Saffron also tolerates some shade, and Bailey’s research so far has found that yields nearly double beneath the partial shade of solar arrays.

“This could provide cash flow value for farmers who want to use solar as an energy source, or who happen to be in an urban agriculture setting,” Bailey said.

Water use offers another reason to keep testing. Bailey said saffron requires roughly half as much water as corn and could potentially survive on rainfall alone, making it an appealing candidate for a region where irrigation water is under pressure.

“This crop is incredibly drought resistant,” Bailey said.

The experiments extend beyond Spur’s rooftops to CSU’s Foothills Campus and Denver Botanic Gardens Chatfield Farms, at the base of the mountains south of Denver. At Chatfield Farms, Lauren Hazlett, one of the head growers working at the solar array, has welcomed the sight of flowers appearing as other plants fade.

“I never thought I’d ever be able to see saffron growing, especially in Colorado—it’s something I always associated with the other side of the world,” she said.

Bousselot and Bailey have also sent bulbs to farmers in Paonia, Pueblo, and Montrose. Their reports will help show how saffron performs in working farm operations and whether its potential benefits carry beyond the research plots.

There is already a long history of finding uses for the spice. Alexander the Great, king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon, reportedly bathed in saffron to help heal battle wounds. Doctors once prescribed it for bubonic plague, and Cleopatra used its fragrance to attract potential suitors. Today, it flavors dishes such as paella and risotto and is increasingly sought after in perfumes.

Modern research is also exploring its medicinal properties. Some studies suggest saffron may support mental health and help alleviate depression, while others have investigated its possible anti-inflammatory effects. Those research areas could add to its commercial appeal, although Colorado’s trials are focused on whether farmers can grow and sell it successfully.

“Up until now, we haven’t really been able to study saffron in Colorado at a deeper level, but the demand is there, and I only think we’ll be talking about it more and more,” Bailey said.

#6461. Solving the Space Junk Crisis Isn't Just About Counting Trash—It’s About Control and Economics

If people ever think about cleaning up space debris, they typically think of something equivalent to a giant garbage truck in the sky, collecting lost astronaut tools and dead satellites then hauling them back down to Earth to be deposited in a landfill. But dealing with space debris doesnât work that way, and a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory, who we typically cover for his work on the Solar Gravitational Lens idea, makes a good argument as to why.

Dr. Turyshev has turned his attention to orbital debris at a critical juncture. According to the filings made to the FCC, SpaceX, the company that runs the largest satellite megaconstellation, had their Starlink satellites perform 144,404 collision avoidance maneuvers in the six months from December 2024 through May 2025. Even accounting for the fact that there are more Starlink satellites in orbit now than ever, that means, on average, each one is having to dodge a potential crash every week.

Fortunately, Starlinks themselves arenât exactly in the âdanger zoneâ of orbit. They typically orbit around 500-600 kilometers, along with other megaconstellations such as Amazonâs Kuiper and Chinaâs Qianfan. In the paper, Dr. Turyshev separates this orbit from those higher up. At 500-600, there is enough atmosphere left that the area is semi self-cleaning - dead satellites and debris in these orbits will burn up in a few years.

Fraser talks about the oribtal dance that keeps satellites from crashing into one another.

Higher up, though, there are bigger problems, both literally and figuratively. At around 850 kilometers, giant rocket stages from launches past lurk with no control, and little to no atmosphere to drag them down in a reasonable time frame. They could stay in orbit for decades or centuries and donât have any means of avoiding one another. When they inevitably collide, they will spray debris both into their own orbit but also into higher and lower ones, potentially causing even greater problems for the lower orbiting communications megaconstellations.

According to European Space Agency Data cited in the paper, about 96 percent of the long-term collision risk comes from these dead objects. And Dr. Turyshev further proves that, even if we stop launching rockets tomorrow, the amount of debris already up there would collide and shatter faster than nature can clear it.

This isnât a surprise to anyone who has been paying attention to the problem of space debris for any length of time. That orbital cascade, commonly known as Kessler Syndrome, has been a long-standing problem orbital dynamicists have been grappling with for decades. According to Dr. Turyshev, controlling it comes down to three separate levers.

Fraser talks about some techniques to remove space debris from orbit.

First, regulators have to ensure that satellites are designed to intentionally deorbit quickly once their missions end. Luckily, they are already moving in that direction, with the FCC recently introducing a rule requiring satellites to clear out within five years of retirement, rather than the twenty-five years that had held sway for the last few decades. According to the paper, if the reliability of disposal rises from 90 to 99 percent and a satelliteâs allowable afterlife is cut to five years, it decreases the environmental hazard by a factor of 50.

A second lever is better vision. Space Situational Awareness (SSA) systems are great at tracking large bulky objects, but terrible at smaller objects the size of a bullet. But even for larger ones, thereâs still a level of âfuzzinessâ that analysts have to deal with, which means they know a general box where an object is in space, but not its exact position. When that box is large, satellite operators waste precious fuel dodging objects that never really posed a threat in the first place.

Rather than trying to track every bolt and nut floating through space, Dr. Turyshev suggests that we need to concentrate on shrinking the uncertainty zone around potential high-risk close calls. That idea aligns directly with the real-world infrastructure upgrades that are happening through NOAAâs Traffic Coordination System for Space (TraCSS), which is expanding its pilot program to reach more commercial operators this year.

Fraser discusses whether there's a limit to how many satellites we can potentially launch.

The third lever is what to do with the semi-permanent debris thatâs already in space. Instead of launching expensive missions to deorbit and grab every single one of them, Dr. Turyshev suggests an alternative he calls Just-in-Time Collision avoidance. If two dead rocket upper stages are about to crash, operators could use ground-based lasers or small swarms of shepherd satellites to move a few meters out of the way just before impact. While not quite as much of a long-term solution (since it simply avoids the immediate problem), it does offer a much less expensive solution than attempting to deorbit everything.

Economic calculations will play a major role in any future space debris solution, and right now the market is broken, as Dr. Turyshev points out. Due to agreements in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, a private cleanup company cannot simply fly up to an abandoned Soviet rocket booster and deorbit it. Technically that rocket booster is still owned by the government that launched it (even if, in this case, that government doesnât technically exist anymore). Also, orbital space suffers from the âtragedy of the commonsâ, as one firm removing a rocket booster benefits all of the other companies with equipment in orbit, despite the cost not being spread amongst them.

Dr. Turyshevâs solution is to create contracts that would pay for verifiable reductions in long-term risk - in other words, it would incentivize companies like Astroscale, which are intending to remove space debris, to remove the most dangerous pieces first. This would be financed by governments, using money from âdisposal bondsâ that pay back if the satellite successfully orbits without active intervention from Astroscale or one of its competitors.

Ultimately, this seems like a reasonable framework to build a long-term plan for space debris mitigation. But there are still some issues - like sheer scale. Even at a 99% successful deorbit rate, with potentially millions of satellites in orbit that would still leave tens of thousands of derelict ones at any given time. And thereâs definitely no clear path forward to a successor to the Outer Space Treaty. But the longer we as a space-faring civilization ignore these issues the worse the problem is going to get. Hopefully this paper helps provide part of the impetus to push towards a formal adopted solution framework. Or at the very least start a more comprehensive conversation about it.

S.G. Turyshev - Orbital Debris in Earth Orbit: Operations, Stability, Control, and Market Formation

UT - What Will It Take To Reach Zero Space Debris?

UT - A New Net-Membrane Could Clean Up Some Tricky Space Debris

UT - Astronomers Use "Blind Stacking" to Uncover Invisible Space Junk Threatening Geosynchronous Orbit

#6459. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”
