#6458. Scientists Discover a Powerful Plastic-Eating Enzyme Hiding in an Ordinary Compost Heap

An enzyme found in compost broke down small amounts of polyurethane foam in laboratory tests, offering an early lead toward gentler ways to recycle a stubborn plastic.

The polyurethane used in mattress foam, shoe soles, and refrigerator insulation is notoriously difficult to recycle on an industrial scale. A very large share of the millions of metric tons produced worldwide ends up in landfills or incinerators, taking potentially reusable material with it.

Nylon presents a similar challenge. Used in clothing, bags, cars, ropes, engine components, and fishing nets, it is another plastic made from crude oil, a finite resource. Researchers want to break both materials down into their pure components so those ingredients can become new polyurethane and nylon. Chemical and biological approaches are making progress, but the solutions emerging from laboratories are not yet ready for industrial use.

Researchers from Aarhus University and the Danish Technological Institute went looking for help among bacteria. Their search took in a Kenyan landfill, a tropical zoo, the guts of wax moth larvae, and a compost heap near Aarhus. The best candidate came from the compost, where a bacterium produced an enzyme with an ability that could prove useful far beyond the heap.

Researchers collected bacteria from plastic-contaminated environments, including a tropical zoo, a landfill in Kenya, compost and larval guts. Using fluorescent probes and fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), they isolated bacteria capable of cleaving chemical bonds found in polyurethane and nylon. The active enzymes were then purified and identified using chromatography, activity assays and mass spectrometry. In total, the researchers identified 10 polyurethane-degrading enzymes and 2 nylon-degrading enzymes. Credit: Rosie Graham / Angewandte Chemie

Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. To find ones that can break down plastic, researchers conventionally search genome databases for gene sequences resembling those of enzymes already known to do the job. That approach has yielded useful enzymes, but there are relatively few known examples to guide the search.

This team used bioprospecting, which means searching nature for organisms and genetic material that could be useful in research or industry. It was the first time researchers had searched on such a large scale and across such varied environments for enzymes capable of degrading polyurethane, also called PUR, and nylon.

The idea came to Andreas Møllebjerg as he prepared to begin a postdoctoral position at what was then the Interdisciplinary Nano Science Center (iNANO) at Aarhus University. He was joining a new project investigating whether natural enzymes could break down plastic. Møllebjerg, a co-author of the resulting study, recently published in Angewandte Chemie, was responsible for collecting bacteria from different environments.

“I suggested looking for suitable enzymes in places where it is warm, because bacteria thrive and grow well there all year round. And preferably somewhere plastic has been present for a long time. A year and a half later, I was on a plane to Kenya, followed by half an hour on the back of a local student’s motorbike on the way to a huge landfill. He helped me collect samples and communicate with the hundreds of people who lived on and off the landfill,” he says.

Møllebjerg and PhD student and co-author Malthe Kjær Bendtsen also traveled 34 kilometers, about 21 miles, to collect plastic waste at Randers Regnskov Tropical Zoo. Møllebjerg bought a bag of wax moth larvae from a pet food shop so the team could investigate enzymes from bacteria in their guts. At a recycling center about 10 kilometers, or 6 miles, from the university, he collected a shovelful of compost.

Those samples gave the researchers millions of bacteria to examine. Finding a useful enzyme required more than showing that a bacterium could react with a convenient laboratory substitute for plastic.

“It was like a three-stage rocket, where we gradually narrowed them down. We started by finding bacteria that could break down the fluorescent model material. Then we isolated the enzymes capable of breaking down exactly that fluorescent material. And finally, we tested the enzymes on increasingly realistic materials,” Bendtsen explains.

This 90-hour time-lapse video shows enzymatic degradation of two different molecules that mimic nylon. The second and fourth vials show CCPUR1 breaking down the two molecules, while the first and third vials show an inactive enzyme. Credit: Samuel Peña Díaz, Aarhus University, and Andreas Sommerfeldt, Danish Technological Institute

For the initial screening, the researchers mixed bacteria with molecules designed to mimic chemical bonds in polyurethane and nylon. The molecules lit up when they encountered a bacterium containing a suitable enzyme. Using fluorescence-activated cell sorting, or FACS, a machine could screen the bacteria and pick out glowing cells at a rate of up to 10,000 per second.

The search identified 29 plastic-degrading bacteria and 12 enzymes with varying abilities to break down polyurethane and nylon. The most promising enzyme was CCPUR1, from the compost bacterium Chelatococcus composti. Its name takes “CC” from the bacterium and “PUR” from PURase, shorthand for polyurethane hydrolase, an enzyme capable of breaking down polyurethane.

Testing on more realistic materials showed both its potential and its limitations. Given polyurethane mattress foam in powdered form, CCPUR1 broke down just under 1% in three days. That leaves a substantial gap between detecting an enzyme’s activity and using it to recycle plastic on an industrial scale.

CCPUR1 nevertheless had several useful characteristics. Its unusually wide binding cleft, a groove where it accommodates the material it acts on, gives large polymer molecules room to fit. Polymers are the long molecules that make up plastics. The enzyme was also particularly stable, withstanding higher temperatures and a range of solvents better than the other candidates.

Its origins in compost offer an explanation for those abilities. Compost contains stubborn plant materials such as wax and lignin, and an enzyme that evolved to break down those substances can also happen to work on plastic. Compost heaps can reach 80°C, or 176°F, so enzymes functioning there need enough stability to withstand the heat.

The team has since worked to improve CCPUR1. In a follow-up study published September 11, 2026, in Chem Catalysis, the researchers collaborated with the University of Porto, using computer simulations and targeted edits to the DNA instructions for making the enzyme.

Within three days, the modified enzyme broke down around 1.4% of the polyurethane in foam from a real shoe sole, without any pretreatment of the plastic. That experiment used a different material from the powdered mattress foam in the original study. Postdoctoral researcher Rosie Graham, who was responsible for testing the enzymes on plastic materials in the laboratory, is the first author of the follow-up study.

The other 11 enzymes could also have a role. They work best on small pieces of plastic and may complement CCPUR1 in future combinations of processes. Because enzymes are selective about what they act on, the researchers envisage using an enzyme cocktail in stages. Polyurethane could first be broken down and washed away, followed by the addition of nylon-degrading enzymes. Chemical methods cannot separate those tasks in the same way.

Making these processes practical may require mechanical and chemical treatments that make the plastic easier for enzymes to attack. Chemical degradation of polyurethane and nylon is itself a major research field, including at Aarhus University. The scale of the remaining challenge is one reason the team compares efficient polyurethane recycling to finding the holy grail.

“But the research highlights the strength of enzymes. Their real advantage when it comes to recycling is that they work under mild conditions, meaning at lower temperatures and pressures than those used in most recycling technologies today,” Graham says.

Reference: “Environmental Identification of Novel Enzymes for Polyurethane and Polyamide Degradation” by Malthe Kjær Bendtsen, Andreas Møllebjerg, Samuel Peña-Díaz, Rosie Graham, Nicolai Claus Petersen, Bjørk Nolsøe Isaksen, Mathias Carstensen, Martin B. Johansen, Andreas Sommerfeldt, Allan R. Petersen, Iddi Khamisi Chuma, Cecilie Ryberg, Thomas Rea Wittenborn, Virginia Gichuru, Huabing Wang, Carsten Scavenius, Alexander Sandahl and Daniel E. Otzen, 26 June 2026, Angewandte Chemie International Edition. DOI: 10.1002/anie.6159643

This work is supported by the Novo Nordisk Foundation through the Challenge Grant NNF22OC0072891 to the Center EnZync.

#6457. Asteroid Bennu's Sample Delivers Another Surprise

One of the most interesting discoveries in recent years is that some of the molecules necessary for life are found on asteroids and comets. Sample return missions from asteroids have shown that these rocky bodies are far more than just rock. They host some of the fundamental building blocksâamino acidsâthat are used to construct proteins.

These discoveries are a collective a-ha! moment. It's becoming clear that some of the precursors for life could be widespread in the Solar System. And if they're widespread in ours, they could be widespread in others. The idea that life could appear elsewhere in the galaxy got a boost.

NASA's OSIRIS-REx was a big part of this when it returned a sample from asteroid Bennu in 2023. Examination of those samples revealed the presence of 14 of the 20 amino acids that make up proteins in Earth life, along with four of the essential building blocks for DNA and RNA.

Now, researchers have compared one of those molecules with the same molecule from another source, the Murchison meteorite, to see how they differ. The research is published in Nature Communications Earth and Environment, and is titled "Nitrogen and intramolecular carbon isotopic measurements of Î²-alanine in samples from asteroid Bennu and the Murchison meteorite." The lead author is OphÃ©lie Mcintosh, a former postdoctoral researcher in Penn Stateâs Department of Geosciences.

âI was genuinely gobsmacked by the enormous isotope difference between two neighboring atom positions within the same molecule. - Katherine Freeman, Professor of Geosciences at Penn State.

"Amino acids are central to prebiotic chemistry, and their abundances and isotopic compositions provide critical constraints on the synthetic mechanisms and environments in which they formed," the authors write. "Samples delivered to Earth from the carbonaceous asteroid (101955) Bennu by NASAâs OSIRIS-REx mission offer an opportunity to investigate amino acids preserved in pristine material unaffected by terrestrial contamination."

Î²-alanine (beta-alanine) isn't used by Earth organisms to build proteins, but it does play other roles in terrestrial life. Finding it in extraterrestrial rocks is interesting because that can provide some insight into pre-biotic chemistry and what conditions were like in the very early Solar System.

This research is focused on the different compositions of Î²-alanine found in Bennu and the Murchison meteorite. Since the Bennu sample was collected and preserved in a sterile capsule before being opened in laboratory conditions, it's especially valuable scientifically.

This sample of the Murchison meteorite sits in the National Museum of Natural History, Washington, D.C. Image Credit: By User:Basilicofresco - Derivative work from Image:Murchison meteorite.jpg, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=4301968

âAmino acids are the building blocks of proteins and peptides, but they are also found in carbon-rich meteorites and asteroid samples, so they can provide a direct link between space chemistry and the origins of life on Earth,â lead author Mcintosh said in a press release. âMost studies focus on the distribution and quantification of amino acids, so our question about how theyâre formed is quite new. We used very unique isotope instruments, including one that exists only at Penn State, to help answer those questions.â

A mission to collect an asteroid sample and return it to Earth is an extremely complicated endeavour. Scientists were hopeful that in the time that passed between planning and launching the mission and getting their hands on the sample, new laboratory techniques would be developed to investigate the sample as deeply and thoroughly as possible. That's what has happened in this case. The researchers were able to measure and compare the different isotopic compositions of Î²-alanine in the Bennu sample and in the Murchison meteorite sample.

They not only compared bulk compositions. In this work, they were actually able to measure and compare isotopic carbon differences in carbon atoms in the same molecule. This level of detail is new.

A device unique to Penn State allowed the measurement of isotopic averages in extremely small samples. It's called pico-CSIA, for Picomolar-scale compound-specific isotope analyses. A second device, a modified GC-Orbitrap (Gas Chromatography-Orbitrap Mass Spectrometer) measured specific compositions at specific locations in Î²-alanine molecules.

âIsotope ratios provide a measurable tag that can link molecules to specific reservoirs or processes,â said paper co-author Christopher House, professor of geosciences at Penn State. âFor our study, isotopes provided clues to an older history for specific atoms in a molecule.â

Looking at isotopic composition is a way to look further back in time for the Î²-alanine's formation history. Typically, researchers are looking at processes inside the asteroid body itself for clues to how it formed.

But examining isotopic composition from molecule to molecule is more fundamental, and carbon plays a critical role. It acts as scaffolding for organic moleculesâEarth life is carbon-based after allâand records isotopic differences between molecules and within molecules. "Intramolecular isotopic measurements, which capture the position-specific carbon isotopic distribution within a molecule, offer a particularly powerful approach as they can reveal reaction mechanisms, constrain precursor reservoirs, and reflect environmental conditions.

âThis intramolecular information provides a much more detailed isotopic fingerprint,â lead author Mcintosh said. âInstead of simply asking whether a molecule is enriched or depleted in a particular isotope, we can investigate how that isotope is distributed within the molecule and use this pattern to distinguish between possible formation pathways.â

This work takes isotopic composition to a whole other level. Especially when used on such a carefully handled sample as that from Bennu.

âBeing able to analyze the isotope values for each carbon and nitrogen within the beta-alanine molecule is a dream for geochemistry,â House said. âAnd here it is coupled to the ability to study a pristine asteroid sample returned to Earth by NASA.â

The isotope values from atom to atom within the same molecule were wildly different, which came as a surprise to the researchers. They may have formed before Earth did.

There was a lot of waiting and anticipation leading up to Bennu's successful sample collection maneuver. Once it was complete, there was more anticipation of the sample's arrival on Earth, and what we'd learn from it. That's partly what makes this research so interesting. Credit: NASA Goddard

âI was genuinely gobsmacked by the enormous isotope difference between two neighboring atom positions within the same molecule,â said project principal investigator Katherine Freeman, Professor of Geosciences at Penn State. âThe preservation of such startling differences is an indicator of the primordial nature of these molecules. We are working with molecules formed at the very dawn of the solar system, possibly even before the formation of Earth.â

The intramolecular isotope differences show that, while their formation pathways were the same, they took place in much different environments, or in different batches. It shows that the same chemical can form in different environments in the protoplanetary disk, and that the disk is spatially heterogeneous.

âOne of the main things we discovered, for both glycine and beta-alanine, is that they might have formed in different environments or places in the solar system,â Mcintosh said. âThis broadens our understanding of the type of environments where you can form those very important molecules for prebiotic chemistry.â

The figure below shows elevated 13C in the Bennu sample, and it's particularly important. "The substantially greater 13C enrichment of the carboxyl carbon in Bennu is consistent with the incorporation of carbon from isotopically distinct precursor reservoirs, potentially reflecting differences in the local chemical environments in which Î²-alanine or its precursors formed," the authors write.

This summary figure shows the carbon isotopic compositions across Solar System bodies, including Bennu (blue diamonds) and Murchison (grey squares). The figure presents bulk carbon values in different planetary bodies. Carbon is important because life is carbon-based, and it's like the structural scaffolding for organic molecules. Within a single molecule, carbon records isotopic differences in a way that other atoms like nitrogen and hydrogen don't. Notice the he greater 13C in carboxyl carbon (COOH) in Bennu, which is particularly important. Image Credit: Mcintosh, O.M., Baczynski, A.A., Rasmussen, C. et al. Nitrogen and intramolecular carbon isotopic measurements of Î²-alanine in samples from asteroid Bennu and the Murchison meteorite. Commun Earth Environ (2026).

âWhen you compare the Bennu and Murchison samples, the carbon isotope average is so close that when you factor in margin of error, theyâre basically the same,â Mcintosh said. âBut when you look at intramolecular carbon, theyâre completely different.â

"The samples display similar intramolecular isotope distributions, consistent with a common synthetic route, but differ markedly in their position-specific carbon and nitrogen isotope compositions," the authors explain.

That means the source materials were distinct isotopically. So they must have came from different locations and environments in the young Solar System. The authors say that the differences are hard to reconcile with any known processes taking place inside parent bodies. Instead, they reflect different chemical pathways in different parts of the protoplanetary disk.

An illustration of a protoplanetary disk. This work shows that the same organic molecules can form in different parts of the disk, though with different isotopic compositions. This suggests that prebiotic chemistry can form in a wider variety of conditions. Image Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/T. Pyle (SSC) - February, 2005

âBeta-alanine is a prominent example of the amazingly diverse collection of amino acid-like molecules found in space samples,â Freeman said. âIt can help us understand why there are so many different types of these compounds and where and how they were made. Ultimately, this helps us understand ways that space organics potentially shaped the unique chemistry in life.â

These results could also be helpful as missions to detect and study potential biosignatures elsewhere in the Solar System are launched. Missions to Jupiter's icy moons could benefit from these results, for example.

"Additionally, isotopic analyses of amino acids and other prebiotic molecules in Bennu samples and other pristine astromaterials provide a critical abiotic baseline for the search and identification of chemical biosignatures within our Solar System.

In a key coastal area of Peru, violence was low despite the practice of human sacrifice.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite engaging in human sacrifice, the people who lived in the Lambayeque Valley of northern Peru had low levels of violence, a new study of their remains finds.

Human sacrifice occurred in the valley over the millennia. It's thought that at least some of these mass sacrifices were attempts to appease the gods in the wake of El Niño, a periodic weather phenomenon that can lead to intense rains and flooding in Peru and droughts in other parts of South and Central America.

"We have one example at the site of Sicán where around [A.D.] 1050/1100, around 200 individuals were killed and ritualistically buried during an intense El Niño event," study co-author Haagen Klaus, an anthropology professor at George Mason University in Virginia, told Live Science in an email.

Other human sacrifice findings include more than 200 children found near the modern-day town of Huanchaco who were sacrificed sometime between 600 and 800 years ago, possibly during an El Niño.

However, despite the occurrence of human sacrifice, levels of violence unrelated to sacrifice were actually quite low in the Lambayeque Valley. In the study, scientists analyzed the skeletal remains of 1,519 people from the Lambayeque Valley who lived between roughly 1500 B.C. and A.D. 1800, and whose remains were preserved enough to detect signs of violent trauma, including interpersonal violence.

A skull showing blunt force trauma that dates to the Chimu period, roughly 1375 to 1490.

Of these skeletons, "only 25 (1.6%) exhibited traumatic lesions consistent with interpersonal conflict, and 77 exhibited post-cranial traumatic lesions consistent with accidental trauma (5.1%)," Klaus and co-author Thomas Snyder, a bioarchaeologist at New York University, wrote in the paper, which was published Nov. 8 in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

The team didn't find any link between a person's sex and violence, they noted. The findings mean that despite the presence of human sacrifice, the amount of violence unrelated to sacrifice was low. This leaves a question: Why?

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A healed fracture on the left leg of a person who lived sometime between 1000 to 650 B.C. The fracture may have been from an accident.

"Ritual violence may have alleviated non-ritual violence by creating spaces where social tensions could get worked out in a few different ways," Klaus said.

It's important to remember that other areas of Peru also practiced human sacrifice but didn't have the same low levels of interpersonal violence. Klaus noted that areas in the Peruvian highlands sometimes had higher rates of interpersonal violence. In their paper, Klaus and Snyder noted that societies that originated in the highlands, such as the Tiwanaku, Wari and Inca had to grapple with poorer soils and cold temperatures, and these challenges may have been a factor in increasing the levels of interpersonal violence.

The "evidence of sub-lethal and lethal violence forceful enough to break bone is significantly higher in some areas of Peru's highlands," Klaus said. He and Snyder noted in their paper that the inhabitants of the Lambayeque Valley may have had better access to marine and water resources, such as seafood and rivers that could be used for agricultural irrigation, than those who lived in highland areas. Access to these resources may have helped alleviate interpersonal violence in the valley by providing more food resources, they wrote.

Aside from practicing human sacrifice, people in the valley may have engaged in other practices that helped lower levels of interpersonal violence, researchers who were not involved in the new study told Live Science.

Environmental conditions may have helped reduce conflict or there could be "really unusual cultural practices in this region of avoiding or mediating conflict — both between and within groups," Elizabeth Arkush, an anthropology professor at the University of Pittsburgh, said in an email.

Constanza Ceruti, an anthropologist and explorer with the National Geographic Society, said in an email that she's glad that researchers are studying human sacrifices "after decades of being ignored as a taboo topic in academic discussion." She praised the study’s large sample size and noted that human sacrifice is a "phenomenon primarily associated [with] the manipulation and concentration of power by elites."

Jordi Rivera Prince, an anthropology professor at Tulane University, said that the findings dovetail with her excavations in the region, where she has "found little evidence of violent trauma during the Salinar (400-200 BCE), a period of great social change in the Andes."

Weston McCool, an archaeology professor at Cal Poly, said in an email that the newly published paper "is an interesting study that provides additional evidence for a sharp break in patterns of violence between the Andean coast and highlands." He noted that it "supports the hypothesis that coastal populations were buffered from terrestrial environmental downturns in ways that highland populations were not. The nature of that resilience, however, remains an important question for future research."

Snyder, T. J., & Klaus, H. D. (2026). Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, 5, 1889466. https://doi.org/10.3389/fearc.2026.1889466

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6454. A Brief-ish History of METI. Part III: The Legacy of Frank Drake & Carl Sagan

Welcome back to our continuing series on the Brief-ish History of METI, where we examine the rise, development, and possible implications of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI). In our first installment, we explored some of the foundational principles, how METI emerged as a possible answer to the "SETI Paradox," and the earliest experiments. In our second, we looked at the pioneering work of Cornell Professor Frank Drake, the "father of SETI," and how his efforts led to the first true experiment in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI): Project Ozma and the Arecibo Message.

We also touched on how these efforts led to his lifelong collaboration with fellow Cornell Professor and famed science communicator Carl Sagan. Today, we will see how this collaboration attracted the attention of NASA and led to the most ambitious projects to send messages to space, ones that might even be found by an extraterrestrial civilization (ETC) someday. These are none other than the Pioneer Plaques and the Voyager Golden Records, which are now in the outer Solar System or have entered interstellar space.

As noted in our last installment, Carl Sagan and Frank Drake first met in 1961, a year after Project Ozma took place. To build on the momentum the experiment created, Drake organized an informal symposium at the Green Bank Observatory (where Ozma was conducted) in 1961. To prepare for the event, Drake formulated an equation that summarized the challenges SETI researchers faced. This became known as the Drake Equation, which remains foundational to the fields of SETI and METI.

The equation states that the number of extraterrestrial civilizations in our galaxy that we could communicate with (N) depends on several variables. These include the annual rate of star formation in the galaxy (R*), the fraction of those stars with planets (fp), the number of planets with conditions suitable for life (ne), the fraction of planets that will develop intelligence (fi), the fraction of planets with intelligent life that will develop transmission technologies (fc), and the average length of time a civilization will be able to produce signals (L). Mathematically, the equation is expressed as:

As one of many prominent scientists attending the symposium, Sagan was impressed with Drake's theories and advocacy for using radio astronomy to search for possible ETCs. However, their interactions predated this meeting and included correspondence when both were young graduate astronomy students. Sagan became aware of Drake when he heard of his work measuring Venus's high temperature. After this meeting, the two became close colleagues and professors at Cornell University, where they went on to collaborate on several landmark projects.

In the early 1970s, the last Apollo mission successfully landed astronauts on the Moon (Eugene A. Cernan, Harrison H. Schmitt, and Ronald E. Evans). This historic accomplishment effectively ended the "Space Race," and NASA was busy contemplating its next moves. It was decided that the Pioneer program, which had sent nine probes to explore the Moon, Venus, Mars, and Mercury between 1958 and 1968, should shift focus to the outer Solar System, exploring the Main Asteroid Belt, Jupiter, Saturn, and the interstellar medium.

This made the probes especially significant, as they would be the first missions to achieve escape velocity from the Solar System. For this reason, journalist and science correspondent Eric Burgess (who was also the Pioneer program's chronicler) suggested that the probes carry a message, should an extraterrestrial species find them someday. Burgess approached Carl Sagan with the idea after hearing him lecture about communicating with extraterrestrial intelligence at a conference in Crimea.

Sagan was enthusiastic about the idea and approached Frank Drake to help design a message that could be interpreted by an ETC. NASA agreed to the plan and gave them three weeks to prepare it, and the two decided to create plaques that could be mounted on the Pioneer 10 and 11 missions. Linda Salzman Sagan, Carl Sagan's wife at the time, prepared the artwork, with additional contributions from space artist and science journalist Jon Lomberg, a long-time collaborator of Sagan's.

The result was the Pioneer Plaques, a pair of six-by-nine-inch (~23 cm by 15.25 cm) gold-anodized aluminum plates. Each contained an engraved pictorial message identifying the probes' place of origin, who sent them, and when they were sent. From top to bottom, left to right, the message included the following details:

A detailed view of the visual message on the Pioneer plaques, developed by Carl Sagan and Frank Drake. Credit: NASA Ames

The Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11 probes launched on March 2nd, 1972, and April 5th, 1973 (respectively), becoming the first robotic missions to explore beyond Mars and the Main Asteroid Belt. The Pioneer Plaques have the distinction of being humanity's first interstellar message of greetings. But in a few years' time, Sagan and Drake would take things a step further, creating something that was meant to convey what life on Earth was like.

The success of the Pioneer 10 and 11 missions motivated NASA to contemplate an even more ambitious mission: dual probes to explore the planets of the outer Solar System. The twin Voyager 1 and 2 probes would launch in the summer of 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment of the outer planets. The mission would conduct close-up studies of Jupiter, Saturn, Saturn's rings, and larger moons. But as the mission progressed, NASA chose to use the alignment to include Uranus and Neptune - what came to be known as the "Grand Tour."

Since these missions would also achieve escape velocity from the Solar System, NASA decided to follow the precedent established with the Pioneer Plaques. This led Voyager project manager John R. Casani to suggest that the Voyager 1 and 2 probes also carry a "message in a bottle" containing information about humanity. He delegated the task to Carl Sagan, who was joined again by Frank Drake and Linda Salzman Sagan, and the three created a metal phonograph record containing information encoded in its grooves.

A record was chosen because it would outlast magnetic tape in the outer-space environment. This time, Sagan and crew were given six weeks to create the records and a budget of $1,500, the equivalent of about 8,780 USD today, though Sagan and his colleagues contributed money of their own. The fruits of their labors were the Voyager Golden Records, a series of 12-inch (30.5 cm) gold-plated copper disks containing sounds and images that portrayed the diversity of life and culture on Earth.

The outer cases were etched with pictograms (see above) similar to the Pioneer Plaques, showing where the probes came from. They also contained instructions for playing the record. In the upper left corner of the case, there is a drawing of the phonograph record and the stylus in the correct position for playing it. Around it, conveyed in binary arithmetic, are the time it takes for the record to complete one rotation (3.6 seconds), the total duration (1 hour), and how it should be played from the outside in.

The upper-right corner contains instructions for constructing pictures from the record. From top to bottom, these include a representation of the signal that indicates the start of a picture, how the signals must be grouped as a series of 512 vertical lines per picture, and what the first image looks like (a circle) to confirm the signals are being processed correctly. The drawing in the lower left-hand corner of the cover is the pulsar map (similar to the Pioneer Plaques) and a drawing of the hyperfine transition of neutral hydrogen.

The Voyager Golden Record (right) and its protective casing with instructions on how to play along with information about its origin (left). Credit: NASA

The record contains 115 encoded images that show human anatomy (a silhouette of a man and a pregnant woman), the structure of DNA, demonstrations of eating and drinking, major locations on Earth, sports and leisure, our planet's geography, and mathematical/scientific concepts. It also contains sound recordings of greetings in 55 languages, whale calls, and music from various cultures and eras (including Beethoven and Chuck Berry). Said then-President Jimmy Carter of the Records:

This is a present from a small, distant world, a token of our sounds, our science, our images, our music, our thoughts and our feelings. We are attempting to survive our time so we may live into yours.

The cover also features a "radioactive clock" in the form of an electroplated uranium-238 sample. Since this element has a half-life of 4.51 billion years, the recipients can calculate how long the probe has been in space. Unlike the Pioneer Plaques, the Voyager Golden Records had a dual purpose: as a message to any extraterrestrial civilization that intercepted them, or as a time capsule for future generations of human explorers should they find them first. As Sagan noted at the time:

The spacecraft will be encountered, and the record played only if there are advanced spacefaring civilizations in interstellar space, but the launching of this 'bottle' into the cosmic 'ocean' says something very hopeful about life on this planet.

Based on its current trajectory and velocity, Pioneer 10 will reach Aldebaran, a star roughly 65 light-years away in the Taurus constellation, in over two million years. Meanwhile, Pioneer 11 is headed for the Aquila constellation and will pass near one of its stars in about 4 million years. On August 25th, 2012, Voyager 1 made history by becoming the first probe to exit the heliosphere and enter interstellar space. Voyager 2 exited from a different location on November 5th, 2018, becoming the second.

They will be joined by Pioneer 10 and 11 probes around 2057, though this will be difficult to verify since both probes are unpowered and cannot send data back to Earth. These plaques and records are unique in that they remain humanity's first attempts to send physical messages into space intended for extraterrestrial recipients and/or future generations. They also established a legacy that continues to this day and is part of a larger debate surrounding the ethics of METI.

This illustration shows the positions of NASA's Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes outside the heliosphere, a protective bubble created by the Sun that extends well past Pluto's orbit. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

These missions have also inspired debate about what a modern message should be and have inspired some experiments. In a series of NASA-led studies that appeared in the AGU journal Earth and Space Science, an international team of scientists proposed what a modern Golden Record should contain. In the first study, titled "Message in a BottleâAn Update to the Golden Record: 1. Objectives and Key Content of the Message," the team summarized the importance of the "Message In A Bottle" (MIAB) and what should motivate future efforts:

These records not only offer a snapshot of Earth and human civilization but also represent our desire to establish contact with advanced alien civilizations. Our goal is to share our collective knowledge, emotions, innovations, and aspirations in a way that provides a universal, yet contextually relevant, understanding of human society, the evolution of life on Earth, and our hopes and concerns for the future. Through this time and space traveling capsule, we also strive to inspire and unify current and future generations to celebrate and safeguard our shared human experience.

Modern attempts to fashion a MIAB include the message attached to the Europa Clipper mission, currently en route to rendezvous with Jupiter and study its moon Europa. The message was unveiled in March 2024, about seven months before the mission launched, and consists of a triangular tantalum plaque - known as the Europa Clipper Vault Plate - measuring about 18 x 28 cm (about 7 x 11 inches) that features graphic elements on both sides. The inward-facing side features an engraving of U.S. Poet Laureate Ada LimÃ³n's handwritten "In Praise of Mystery: A Poem for Europa."

The outward-facing panel contains etchings of soundwaves that illustrate Earth's connection to Europa. Each etching is the word "water" spoken in one of 103 languages from around the world, which were converted into waveforms. Each waveform radiates outward from a symbol representing the sign for "water" in American Sign Language (ASL). Since the Europa Clipper is searching for possible evidence of life inside the icy moon, the Drake Equation is also etched into the plate.

Rather than being a message intended for extraterrestrials, this "Golden Record for Europa" honors the spirit of the original records, aiming to spark the imagination and offer a unifying vision. As Lori Glaze, director of the Planetary Science Division at NASA, said in a statement:

The content and design of Europa Clipper's vault plate are swimming with meaning. The plate combines the best humanity has to offer across the universe â science, technology, education, art, and math. The message of connection through water, essential for all forms of life as we know it, perfectly illustrates Earth's tie to this mysterious ocean world we are setting out to explore.

The "Message in a Bottle" plate attached to the Europa Clipper mission, currently en route to Jupiter. Credit: NASA

These messages highlight the major shift in consciousness that accompanied the Space Age. With humans now venturing out into space and exploring beyond Earth's orbit, a new awareness was taking root, one which saw humanity in cosmological terms. We were not only pondering the existence of extraterrestrial intelligence and civilizations. We were also considering how we might communicate with them and fashioning messages that might someday reach them... unless we get to them first!

These messages also raise the question of whether ETCs might be doing the same: could advanced civilizations be sending probes with their own messages, ones that share what life is like on their respective homeworlds? The fact that we have sent out four MIABs to date has motivated some scientists to consider the possibility that space is littered with derelict spacecraft, some of which could be messenger probes. Perhaps some of them are even here in our Solar System, lingering near Earth or in the far expanse of the Kuiper Belt.

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. His work is featured in The Ross 248 Project and Interstellar Travel edited by NASA alumni Les Johnson and Ken Roy. He also hosts the podcast series Stories from Space on Patreon. He lives in beautiful British Columbia with his wife and family. For more information, check out his website.

#6453. Scientists Discover a Hidden Immune System Difference That Could Explain Why Obesity Affects Men and Women Differently

Scientists have discovered that immune cells in fat tissue behave differently in males and females, potentially helping explain sex-specific responses to obesity.

A type of immune cell best known for its role in allergies and asthma may help explain why obesity affects males and females differently. Researchers at the University of California, Riverside found that certain immune cells in fat tissue appear to protect female mice from obesity-related inflammation, while others become more inflammatory in males fed a high-fat diet.

The findings, published in PNAS Nexus, challenge the long-held assumption that these cells, called eosinophils, perform a relatively narrow range of functions. Instead, their effects may depend on their molecular characteristics, biological sex, and interactions with neighboring immune cells.

Using high-resolution single-cell sequencing, scientists identified six distinct eosinophil populations in adipose (fat) tissue. Each population displayed different patterns of gene activity, suggesting that eosinophils perform specialized functions rather than acting as a single, uniform group.

“Eosinophils are more complex than we once thought,” said Meera Nair, a professor of biomedical sciences at the UCR School of Medicine who co-led the research with biomedical scientist Adam Godzik. “Some populations can protect against obesity, and if we can identify and activate the pathways that produce these protective cells, we may find new ways to improve metabolic health.”

In female mice, researchers identified a protective eosinophil population that communicated more effectively with macrophages, another class of immune cells found in fat tissue. This relationship appeared to be supported by RELM alpha, a protein produced by macrophages that may help maintain protective immune activity. Earlier experiments showed that supplying RELM alpha to mice had protective effects, providing additional evidence for its role in regulating the immune environment.

Male mice showed a different response to a high-fat diet. Their fat tissue tended to contain more eosinophil populations associated with inflammation, and these cells displayed gene-expression patterns that suggested weaker protective functions.

“This means the relationship between eosinophils and obesity is not simply a matter of how many eosinophils are present,” said Rebecca E. Ruggiero-Ruff, a postdoctoral researcher in Nair’s laboratory and co-first author of the study. “Their functional characteristics and how they communicate with other immune cells are also critical.”

Although eosinophils have been detected in the fat tissue of people with obesity, scientists have not yet established whether they perform the same protective or inflammatory functions observed in mice. Determining whether similar cell populations exist in humans could help researchers investigate treatments that influence specific immune pathways rather than broadly altering immune activity.

“A drug may not activate the same pathways or produce the same effects in males and females, particularly when it targets the immune system,” said co-first author Xinru Qiu, a postdoctoral researcher in Godzik’s laboratory. “We need to investigate sex-specific biology more thoroughly so that treatments can be optimized for different patients.”

The researchers are now developing three-dimensional adipose organoids, laboratory-grown structures that reproduce certain features of human fat tissue. These models could allow scientists to examine how eosinophils interact with fat cells and macrophages, and whether modifying those interactions can encourage healthier tissue responses.

“We ultimately hope to develop human adipose organoids that will allow us to investigate whether manipulating immune-cell communication can promote healthier tissue responses,” said Godzik, a professor of biomedical sciences and the Bruce D. and Nancy B. Varner Presidential Endowed Chair in Cancer Research.

Reference: “Single-cell heterogeneity of adipose eosinophils is shaped by sex and RELMα and linked to macrophage communication networks in obesity” by Rebecca E Ruggiero-Ruff, Xinru Qiu, Lauren Vance, Yuxin He, Djurdjica Coss, Adam Godzik and Meera G Nair, 24 October 2026, PNAS Nexus. DOI: 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag365

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health, UCR School of Medicine, and California Institute for Regenerative Medicine.

#6452. Your Brain Chemistry Could Change How You Understand Language

A single word can overturn your understanding of a sentence, and your brain chemistry may shape how hard you work to make sense of it again.

Even a single word can change the meaning of an entire sentence, forcing the brain to rethink what it just read. But how efficiently the brain handles these grammatical surprises may depend partly on its chemistry.

A study published in PNAS found that increasing dopamine and noradrenaline (catecholamines) strengthened a brain response associated with untangling ambiguous grammar. Researchers led by the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics (MPI-PL) in Nijmegen observed the largest effects in healthy adults with lower baseline working memory capacity.

“Catecholamines are known to regulate attention, working memory, and cognitive control, but their role in language remains poorly understood,” says Peter Hagoort, senior investigator and director emeritus of MPI-PL’s Neurobiology of Language Department and the Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behavior.

“Our earlier work suggested that catecholamines can affect semantic aspects of sentence comprehension. Whether these neuromodulatory systems also influence syntactic processing—how the brain combines words into grammatical structures—was largely unknown.”

Understanding a sentence involves more than knowing what its words mean. Readers also have to work out how those words fit together, sometimes revising an interpretation as new information arrives. The researchers used temporarily ambiguous “garden-path” sentences to examine that process.

Consider “The fan attacked the drummer, and the guitarist packed the instruments up.” When the words appear one at a time, readers may initially group “the drummer and the guitarist” together as the people being attacked. The word “packed” reveals that the guitarist is instead performing a separate action, requiring readers to rebuild their interpretation.

To test whether brain chemistry influences this revision, the team recruited 30 healthy adults. Each completed two sessions, once after taking methylphenidate, a stimulant commonly prescribed for ADHD that increases catecholamine levels, and once after taking a placebo.

Participants read ambiguous and unambiguous sentences and answered comprehension questions after each one. Meanwhile, researchers recorded their brain activity using EEG (electroencephalography), allowing them to examine the response at the precise word that exposed the grammatical ambiguity.

After methylphenidate, participants showed a stronger P600 response at the critical word, such as “packed.” This well-known EEG signal is associated with demanding grammatical processing and reflects increased cognitive effort. Its enhancement suggests that higher catecholamine levels changed how the brain recruited resources to resolve the sentence.

The increase was greatest among participants whose working memory capacity was lower before treatment.

“The findings suggest that catecholaminergic systems contribute to the dynamic allocation of cognitive resources during syntactic processing,” says Hagoort. “Their influence on language therefore appears to extend beyond semantic processing to syntactic unification, and the magnitude of this effect may depend on individual baseline working memory performance.”

“The results support the development of neuropharmacolinguistics as a field linking neuromodulatory systems to language processing.”

Reference: “Neuropharmacology of language: ERP evidence for catecholaminergic modulation of syntactic processing” by Yingying Tan, Ashley G. Lewis, Iris C. Schmits, Robert-Jan Verkes, Roshan Cools and Peter Hagoort, 22 October 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2606806123

#6451. Euclid's First Data Release: A Stepping Stone to its 3D Map of the Sky

The ESA's Euclid has already teased us with some early results. In the past it's given us a small, 60 square degree of the sky created with a few days of observations. Those images showed individual targets from the Horsehead Nebula to the Perseus cluster of galaxies.

But now we have data from more than one year of the telescope's observations, named DR1-Foundation. DR-1 Foundation covers a sky area as large as about 9,500 full moons, and captures light from more than one billion objects. It took about 13 months to gather all this data.

Understanding dark energy and dark matter means studying as much of the Universe as possible. The effects of dark energy and dark matter are felt at large scales, and by constructing an image of galaxy superclusters and the filaments they exist on, as well as the voids between those filaments, Euclid will lead to new understandings of both dark energy and dark matter.

There are other efforts to map this structure, some dating back decades. DESI, the Dark Energy Survey Instrument, has created the largest 3D map so far, but Euclid's will be larger. Euclid's will have more depth and volume, and since it's space-based while DESI is ground-based, it won't have to deal with atmospheric interference and will have a higher resolution.

This data release is from the Euclid's Wide and Deep Surveys, two surveys that will form the backbone of its 3D map. Even though the data covers 1900 square degrees of the sky, they only represent about 14% of the sky the space telescope will cover in its six-year mission.

This image shows Euclid's Wide Survey in light yellow and its Deep Survey in darker yellow. The Deep Survey are targeted regions within the Wide Survey. They're overlain on a star map from Gaia and a dust map from Planck. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA; ESA/Gaia/DPAC; ESA/Planck Collaboration. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence

The Wide Survey is Euclid's primary campaign and will cover almost half of the galactic sky. It's an imaging and spectrographic survey in visible and near-infrared. It's the telescope's main cosmology survey and will cover a large volume to constrain dark energy and dark matter.

The Deep Survey serves a different purpose. It'll find fainter objects like dwarf galaxies, low-mass galaxies, and tidal tails, as well as high redshift galaxies and quasars. It will serve to calibrate the Wide Survey, and will provide its own, separate science based on its higher density of sources.

Basically, the Wide Durvey provides the greater volume, and the Deep Survey looks more closely and gives more depth. The two combined are needed for a cosmological survey.

Part of the release includes Euclid's image of the core of the Messier 81 galaxy group. This image shows part of that, centered on the Messier 81 galaxy, the group's largest member. The smaller NGC 3077 is on the left, which is also a member, as are many other small members spread across the image. Wispy blue clouds, sometimes called 'galactic cirrus clouds' are also visible. An irregular dwarf galaxy is also visible in diffuse blue to the left. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre and E. Bertin. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence

Euclid also delivered an image of NGC 1291, a stunning ring galaxy about 33 million light years away. It's also called the Golden Eye galaxy, and it has an inner ring and an outer ring, as well as an inner bar. It's inner and outer rings may be because of a merger with a gas-rich galaxy in the past.

This is Euclid's image of NGC 1291, a ring galaxy that faces us head-on. It's about 33 million light years away, and highlights Euclid's power. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre and E. Bertin. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence

Euclid also captured images of Abell 3128. It's 800 million light years away and contains hundreds of individual galaxies. Massive clusters like this one are important probes for dark energy and dark matter, but especially for dark matter. They serve as important gravitational lenses and reveal a lot about where dark matter is concentrated. They can help cosmologists test Lambda-Cold Dark Matter, which is the standard Big Bang theory of the Universe. They also help Euclid calibrate itself.

This is the Abell 3128 cluster, part of the Horologium supercluster. Horologium is home to more than 30 smaller clusters, and Abell 3128 is one of its richest members. Abell holds spirals and ellipticals, and a gravitational lens is in the middle, warping and magnifying the light from a distant background galaxy. The image shows only a fraction of Abell 3128, and also part of another galaxy cluster named ACT-CL J0330-5227; while in reality the two clusters are separated by a huge distance of around 5 billion light-years, they overlap here in our line of sight. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre and E. Bertin. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence

We're only at the appetizer of the visual and scientific feast that Euclid will deliver. By the time it's completed, its 3D map of the sky will be visually entrancing and full of science. It's already discovered a new comet, the most ancient quasar in the Universe, and new images of the Milky Way's over-populated center.

It's off to a strong start and will only get better.

#6449. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#6448. Tears of the Lion: Catching the 2026 Leonid Meteors

Why you should watch for the November Leonid meteors this year.

Itâs always worth being vigilant when skywatching in mid- to late November. Every year, a few Leonid meteors punctuate the November sky morning sky around the 17th. These silent harbingers are only a hint at the showerâs true storm potential, which culminates once every three decades.

The Leonid meteor shower can put on a true spectacle, and while 2026 isnât expected to be a âstorm year,â we could be due for some enhanced activity in the late 2020s going into the early 2030s.

The source of the Leonid meteor shower is periodic comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. On a 33 year orbit, comet 55P reaches perihelion 0.975 Astronomical Units (AU) from the Sun just inside Earthâs orbit once again on May 20, 2031.

Hubble captures Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Credit: NASA/HST/STScI

In 2026 the Moon phase is favorable at 41% illuminated, reaching 1st quarter phase a day after the showerâs peak night on November 16-17th. This means the Moon sets in the west, right as the radiant rises to the east.

The peak of the 2026 Leonids is set for November 17th at 3:00 Universal Time (UT), favoring Europe towards dawn, and North America just a few hours later. While 2026 is projected to be a 20 meteors per hour peak year, you just never know what a particular shower might have in store.

The Leonids are also real fast movers, approaching the Earth nearly head-on with a combined velocity of close to 70 kilometers per second. This is very near the theoretical maximum for inner solar system meteors. Most years only see a paltry 20 or so meteors per hour, though when the parent comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle is near perihelion, great storms are possible.

The Leonids hail from the backwards, question mark-shaped âSickle of Leoâ asterism. The radiant tracks from the +3rd magnitude star Epsilon Leonis past the bright double star Algieba in November. If you can trace a meteorâs flight back to this region, itâs a Leonid.

As an added treat in 2026, the planets Mars and Jupiter are very nearby, along with the bright star Regulus and the antihelion point towards which our planet is currently headed.

The rising Leonid radiant in 2026. Credit: Stellarium.

The Leonids top out with great outbursts every 33 years. A loose definition for a âmeteor stormâ is when the zenithal hourly rate (ZHR) tops out at about a 1,000 per hour, which is a fast-paced rate of one meteor every 3-4 seconds. Keep in mind, the ZHR is an extrapolated, ideal rate, assuming dark skies with the showerâs radiant directly overhead at the zenith. Most observers will always see less in reality, as fainter meteors slip by.

Records of the Leonids go all the way back to Arab annuals dating from 902 AD. 1833 saw an historic storm from the shower, as frightened residents along the U.S. Eastern Seaboard awoke to a sky awash in meteors. This single event was not only responsible in part for several religious movements of the day in the U.S., but also helped to push the modern scientific understanding of meteors from a purely atmospheric phenomenon to one originating from space.

A depiction of the Great Leonid Storm of 1833, depicted in 1889 by Adolf Vollmy. Credit: Public Domain.

The morning of November 17, 1966 saw a formidable performance from the shower, with observed rates over the southwestern U.S. topping out at an estimated 160,000 per hour (!)

I still remember catching the 1998 Leonids from the deserts of Kuwait, a year before the advertised outburst in 1999. The meteors lit up the desert floor just seconds apart towards sunrise with brilliant photo-flash flares. The spectacle continued right up until dawn. To date, it was still one of the best meteor showers Iâve ever witnessed.

Are we in for another great âmeteor stormâ in or around 2033? Well, we passed the mid-point in 2017. We did see a steady uptick in meteor activity through the late 1990s leading up to 1999. A caveat, however is in order with the approach of the Leonids in the early 2030s. Current models suggest we wonât see any great storms on the 2031 and 2064 passes of the comet, with 2099 being the next great âstorm yearâ. We may, however, still see respectable showers in excess of 100 per hour in the early 2030s laid down by older streams, topping the annual Perseid and Geminid meteors.

A Leonid double-shot. Credit: Eliot Herman

Observing a meteor shower is as simple as laying back and watching the sky, no special equipment needed. All you need is clear, dark skies and patience. Youâll see more in the early morning hours, as Earth hurdles headlong into the oncoming meteor stream. Imaging Leonids is a simple as setting up a tripod-mounted DSLR camera equipped with a wide-field lens to take long exposure shots of the sky, and seeing what turns up. An intervalometer hand control works great to automate this process.

An all-sky capture featuring a Leonid meteor. Credit: Eliot Herman.

Finally, be sure to count and record what you see, and send those observations to the International Meteor Organization.

Weâll see what the coming years has in store for the November Leonid meteors. One thing is for certain: youâll see zero meteors if you donât try. Time will tell if the coming years see the Leonids roar once again.

#6447. Scientists Discover California Has Way More Bugs Than Anyone Imagined

California is teeming with thousands of insect species science has yet to name, and its wild places hold more distinct worlds of tiny creatures than researchers realized.

California is home to an astonishing variety of insects, from the deserts of the Mojave to the forests of the Sierra Nevada. But scientists are discovering that the state’s insect diversity is far greater than previously believed.

A new study in Ecography estimates that California supports more than 60,000 insect species, far exceeding earlier estimates. Scientists have formally described only about two-thirds of them. Led by researchers at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, the study also found that nearly every location sampled had its own distinct insect community.

The findings suggest that conserving California’s insect life will require protecting a wide range of habitats. Even places with similar climates and landscapes can harbor different species, making it difficult for any single protected area to represent the state’s extraordinary diversity.

The research is the first publication from the California Insect Barcode Initiative (CIBI), a $6 million project with an ambitious goal: collect and identify every insect species in California. Although insects are the most diverse group of animals on land, they remain underrepresented in large-scale conservation assessments.

Researchers used DNA barcoding on more than one million insect specimens. The technique compares short sections of DNA to help distinguish species, giving scientists a way to investigate diversity that can be difficult to recognize from appearance alone.

The effort brought together the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, California Department of Food and Agriculture, UC Berkeley, UC Riverside, San Diego Natural History Museum, and California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco. Researchers gathered tissue samples from museum collections, deployed Malaise traps across 72 ecoregions, and made collecting expeditions to 454 additional locations statewide.

Museum specimens extended the project’s reach beyond what researchers could collect in the field. Fresh sampling added another essential piece, with volunteers helping keep traps operating week after week. Although Malaise traps capture insects passively, collecting their contents and maintaining them takes sustained effort.

“This is an example of community science. Volunteers stepped forward to help with sampling by managing traps, which we would not have been able to do for continuous weekly sampling,” says study co-author Giar-Ann Kung, the museum’s entomology collections manager.

Kung joined researchers and volunteers across California in setting traps and collecting insects. Some participants maintained sampling sites for years, providing a continuity that the research team could not have achieved alone.

“There are people like Sara Fairchild and Michael Nance who managed a Malaise trap for over three years at a site in the high desert, which is the longest continuous site for the project. That could not have been accomplished without them.”

To explore how insect diversity varies across California, the researchers compared ecoregions, areas grouped by the Environmental Protection Agency according to shared ecosystem characteristics. They used Level 3 classifications, including the Mojave Basin and Range, Southern California Mountains, and Sierra Nevada. Of these regions, the Mojave Basin and Range had the greatest number of insect species.

Although similar environments shared some patterns, each region had its own mix of insects. “The deserts are kind of more similar to each other, and the mountains in northern California are a little bit more similar to each other, but every part of the state hosts a really different insect fauna,” says Dr. Barkdull.

Those differences also appeared at a smaller scale, with individual collecting sites within the same ecoregion harboring distinct insect communities. Together, the findings highlight the need to protect a wide range of California’s wild places.

A DNA analysis has confirmed that a Nazca infant who lived in southern Peru 1,600 years ago had a rare congenital condition called trisomy 13.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Peru have discovered the skeleton of an infant with a rare birth defect that left only one central eye socket in the child's skull. DNA analysis of the remains confirmed a chromosomal abnormality caused the deadly condition in the infant over 1,600 years ago, according to a new study.

"We cannot really say how long this individual survived," study co-author Lars Fehren-Schmitz, an anthropologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told Live Science in an email. But "the burial of this infant suggests that the Nasca treated this individual in death like most other infants."

The skeleton of this female infant was discovered alongside a second one inside a ceramic urn at the archaeological site of Jauranga in Peru's Palpa Valley, where numerous geoglyphs known as the Nazca Lines have been found. Archaeologists uncovered several dozen other burials dated to the Middle Nazca (also spelled Nasca) period (A.D. 325 to 440) at the site, but one of the co-buried infants had an extremely rare condition, researchers wrote in a study published Monday (Nov. 9) in the journal PNAS.

The infant had a very small skull and a single eye socket in the middle of her face, along with other developmental issues of the cranial bones. These traits match modern clinical descriptions of cyclopia, a lethal condition that occurs when the front part of a fetus's brain fails to divide into left and right hemispheres.

This condition can also cause alterations in the nasal structures, resulting in a missing nose or a tube-like nose above the single eye.

A medical illustration from 1891 of two infants with cyclopia.

"The cause of the malformation was present at fertilization, but manifestation occurs around the fourth to fifth week in utero [in the womb], when the frontal lobe of the brain has to divide," study first author Elsa Tomasto-Cagigao, an archaeologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, told Live Science in an email.

Cyclopia is a rare condition, occurring in about 1 out of every 100,000 births. To learn more about the infant's short life, the researchers sequenced her genome. (DNA suggested the infant carried two X chromosomes, typical of a female.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team detected an extra copy of chromosome 13, meaning the infant had a genetic condition called trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome. It's known to be a major chromosomal cause of cyclopia; that said, only a small percentage of trisomy 13 cases involve cyclopia.

While trisomy 13 is associated with advanced maternal age, it is not clear whether that was the case for this infant, Fehren-Schmitz said.

"This condition has been documented in historic and modern anatomical collections, but to my knowledge this is the first archaeological example of this developmental abnormality," Siân Halcrow, a bioarchaeologist at Durham University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

The researchers' estimate of the infant's age at death suggests she may have survived for several weeks or months after birth, Halcrow pointed out. "This raises important questions about how infants with profound congenital differences were cared for and treated in past societies," she said.

The infant was buried in a ceramic urn, the researchers noted in the study, which was a common burial method in the Nazca period, along with a second female infant who had no skeletal abnormalities. "The baby with cyclopia was at the bottom of the jar, while the other baby was on top. Nevertheless, it appears that they were interred in a single event," Tomasto-Cagigao said. The genetic analysis showed that the two infants did not have the same mother.

A burial of two infants in one urn is unusual for this culture, the researchers said, but there is not enough archaeological evidence to conclude that the infant with cyclopia was given a different type of burial.

"The fact that the individual was buried with a 'healthy' individual in a regular cemetery, without any special grave goods, suggests that, to some extent, the individual was not treated differently in death, even though it had such a rare condition," Fehren-Schmitz said. "It was neither 'excluded' because of it nor treated in a 'special' way."

In ancient Andean societies, some people with disabilities took on special societal roles, such as ones associated with religious practices. "If that reflects Nasca society as a whole, we can't say based on one case," Fehren-Schmitz said, "but it does reflect the community this infant was part of, even if only briefly."

#6444. Scientists Develop a Groundbreaking Rechargeable Battery That Runs on Vitamin B12

The same vitamin found in everyday foods could eventually help store surplus renewable electricity, after an experimental zinc-air battery using B12 completed up to 250 recharge cycles.

The search for safer, more sustainable batteries is leading scientists to some unexpected places, including the chemistry of vitamins. Researchers at the University of Córdoba in Spain have found that vitamin B12, a nutrient essential to human health, can also help power a rechargeable battery. Their experimental design completed up to 250 charge and discharge cycles, opening another possibility for future energy storage technology.

The researchers developed a zinc-air battery, which generates electricity through chemical reactions involving zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air. Unlike conventional batteries that store all their reactive materials internally, zinc-air batteries draw oxygen from the environment. This makes them lighter and gives them high energy density, meaning they can store substantial energy relative to their weight. They are already used in small devices such as hearing aids.

Zinc also offers advantages because it is abundant and recyclable. These batteries use nonflammable, water-based electrolytes, making them potentially safer than conventional lithium-ion batteries, whose raw material extraction raises economic, social, and environmental concerns.

Making zinc-air batteries rechargeable, however, presents a challenge. They need a catalyst, a substance that helps chemical reactions proceed, that can support both the production of electricity and the reverse process needed to recharge the battery.

Vitamin B12, also known as cobalamin, offered a possible solution because its molecular structure contains cobalt (III), a form of the metal cobalt that helps drive these reactions. Although better known for its role in nutrition, B12 is produced naturally by certain bacteria and manufactured commercially for food and pharmaceutical applications. Found in foods of animal origin, it is used to address nutritional deficiencies and has also become popular alongside other B vitamins as a hangover remedy because it can help reduce fatigue.

Researcher Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero explained that vitamin B12 “has proven to meet the necessary conditions to act as a good catalyst because, during discharge, it catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water and, during recharging, it promotes the production of oxygen”.

The difficulty was keeping the vitamin inside the battery. Because B12 dissolves readily in water, it could not simply be added to a battery that uses a water-based electrolyte. The researchers solved this problem by attaching the vitamin to single-walled carbon nanotubes, extremely thin carbon structures that hold it in place while allowing it to support the chemical reactions. Their approach mimicked “the process by which amino acids bind together in proteins.”

The prototype was developed by the Physical Chemistry research group (FQM-204) at the University of Córdoba’s Chemical Institute for Energy and the Environment (IQUEMA). As study author Manuel Cano Luna explained, “we looked at the properties we can find in naturally occurring materials to use them in new batteries.”

This is the group’s third battery prototype using a biological molecule as a catalyst. Earlier experiments involved hemoglobin, which contains iron (II), and catalase, which contains iron (III). The key advance with vitamin B12 is that the resulting battery can be recharged, completing up to 250 cycles in the researchers’ tests.

Although the prototype remains experimental, the findings suggest that naturally occurring molecules could contribute to cheaper, more sustainable energy storage systems. With further development, rechargeable zinc-air batteries could eventually help store surplus electricity from renewable energy sources, addressing one of the challenges of transitioning toward cleaner energy.

Reference: “A vitamin B12-based air electrode for high-performance rechargeable zinc–air batteries” by García-Caballero, Valentín, López-León, Miguel, G.
