#6431. Mars May Not Be Dead After All, New Discovery Suggests

Gas above a Martian volcano may come from hidden magma, offering clues to the planet’s remaining heat and its potential to support life underground.

Hydrogen chloride gas usually reaches its highest levels in Mars’s atmosphere during winter in the northern hemisphere, then mostly disappears in summer. Much of that seasonal pattern appears to follow the planet’s dust and water cycles. Above volcanic fissures on the flanks of Alba Mons, researchers found a recurring exception. Localized spikes of the gas appeared in the same place in early northern summer, raising the possibility of a source beneath the ground.

An international research team led by Alexander Trokhimovskiy suggests that the gas could be escaping from hot magma below the region. Its study, published November 4, 2026, in Science Advances, brings together atmospheric measurements and geological evidence to investigate a possible connection to dormant volcanism.

This artist’s impression shows hydrogen chloride gas rising from within Mars’ crust and venting to the atmosphere, where the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter detects it. The animation explains one scenario of how the timing of the hydrogen chloride detection is governed by seasonal water ice. Credit: ESA

The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) first reported hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere in 2021. On Earth, the gas commonly escapes from magmatic vents, making a volcanic source on Mars a possibility worth examining. Using infrared spectrometers in TGO’s Atmospheric Chemistry Suite, researchers detected a strongly localized concentration above Alba Mons just after winter frosts sublimated, turning directly from ice into vapor.

“Looking at the spatial distribution of the seeping, it became instantly obvious to me that there was something volcanic behind it, but it had to be demonstrated,” says Daniel Mège, a professor at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences and co-lead author of the paper. “A huge part of the work consisted of examining all the possible chemical processes going on in the Martian atmosphere. We needed to be rigorous, critical, and creative to explain the presence of hydrogen chloride. The data were complex, but also excellent brain food.”

A closer look at Alba Mons with TGO’s CaSSIS camera revealed fresh, narrow fissures, some hundreds of meters long, associated with changes in surface color. Those features provided geological evidence to consider alongside the gas measurements.

The team proposes that a dormant magma chamber, an underground reservoir of molten rock, could supply gases that rise through the fissures. During winter, when temperatures fall as low as −120°C (−184°F), ice could block their escape. As the ice sublimates in early summer, the openings would allow the gases to reach the atmosphere. The fissures could therefore behave like fumaroles on Earth, vents that release volcanic gases. Deposits left by escaping gases could also explain the discoloration around them.

“The Trace Gas Orbiter was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack. It’s truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere,” Mège says.

Scientists still do not know how active Mars’s volcanoes are. The planet has the largest volcanoes in the solar system, and orbital images suggest that some were active within the last few million years. Seismometers have also detected marsquakes, the Martian equivalent of earthquakes. Both observations point to the possibility of continuing volcanic activity, although no new lava flows or eruptions have ever been observed.

“Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does,” Mège says.

“These findings may prove to be TGO’s greatest success yet,” says Colin Wilson, ESA’s project scientist for the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter.

Magmatic gases such as hydrogen chloride could have been more abundant earlier in Mars’s history, contributing to a thicker atmosphere and a warmer climate that allowed liquid water to cover much of the surface. If molten rock rising through the crust encounters groundwater, it could also create warm niches potentially suitable for life.

“Looking for Martian life in the seeping fissures of the Alba Mons region would make a lot of sense. If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface,” Mège says.

Reference: “Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars” by Alexander Trokhimovskiy, Daniel Mège, Oleg Korablev, Kevin S. Olsen, Anna A. Fedorova, Benjamin Taysum, Pierre-Antoine Tesson, Mikhail Luginin, Franck Montmessin, Pavel Vlasov, Alexey Grigoriev, Juan Alday, Denis Belyaev, Nikolay Ignatiev, Andrey Patrakeev, Nikita Kokonkov, Yuriy Ivanov, Joanna Gurgurewicz, Antoine Pommerol, Gabriele Cremonese and Nicolas Thomas, 4 November 2026, Science Advances. A 2019 astronaut photo shows the near-perfect cone of a highly active volcano poking its heavily scarred and partially snow-covered head above a thick bank of low-lying clouds over the Kuril Islands.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Atlasov Island, off the coast of Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula [50.84755357, 155.56126752]

What's in the photo? The summit of Alaid volcano peeking above a thick layer of low-lying clouds

Who took the photo? An unnamed astronaut on board the International Space Station

This eye-catching astronaut photo shows a towering, highly active Russian volcano poking its head above a thick bank of swirling clouds over the Kuril Islands.

The lofty peak is located on Atlasov Island, the northernmost of the Kuril Islands — a chain of roughly 50 largely uninhabited volcanic landmasses stretching along a fault line that runs between Russia and Japan in the Sea of Okhotsk. Altasov lies 40 miles (65 kilometers) off Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula, which is also renowned for its volcanic activity.

The island consists mainly of a single, massive volcano, called Alaid, which is known for its near-perfect cone shape. Alaid reaches up to 7,497 feet (2,285 meters) above sea level, making it the tallest peak in the Kuril Islands.

Alaid has erupted at least nine times in the past 50 years, including a major outburst in April 1981 that ejected a 1,250-mile-long (2,000 km) plume of thick smoke and ash into the atmosphere, according to the Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program.

Its most recent eruption occurred between September and November 2022, when a river of lava flowed down its flank (see below). During this outburst, the volcano also spit out smoke and ash that was spotted from space alongside another eruption plume coming from the nearby island Paramushir.

Alaid last erupted in November 2022 and unleashed a scorching lava flow down its snow-covered slopes. This photo also shows what Atlasov Island looks like when it is not obscured by clouds.

In the astronaut's photo, roughly half of Atlasov Island rises above a deep, low-lying bank of swirling clouds. The summit of Alaid, crowned by a roughly mile-wide (1.6 km) caldera, is also obscured by clouds. (The volcano was not erupting when the photo was taken.)

Farther down the volcano's flanks are a series of snow-filled gullies carved out by lava flows from previous eruptions. Eagle-eyed viewers may also be able to spot some parasitic cones — small openings where lava burst through in the past — around the edge of the cloud layer, according to NASA's Earth Observatory.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The area surrounding a cluster of parasitic cones on the volcano's northwest flank (top right in the photo) is devoid of vegetation ‪—‬ a result of another major eruption in 1972, which scoured the surrounding landscape with hot ash. A 2009 study revealed fresh signs of recovery in the affected area, but noted that it could take hundreds of years for vegetation to return to pre-eruption levels.

The clouds are not the only thing the island rises above. Alaid is essentially the summit of a much larger underwater volcano that lies beneath the Sea of Okhotsk. The rest of the island has grown around the exposed cone as lava flows have reached sea level and solidified. Millions of years ago, this larger volcano was likely connected to the Kamchatka Peninsula via a land bridge that has since been submerged.

In 1981, a major eruption caused Alaid to unleash a massive plume of smoke and ash that reached up to 1,250 miles long.

Astronauts and satellites have snapped several other stunning shots of intriguing landmasses nearby, including a quartet of end-to-end volcanoes on Simushir Island and a set of volcanic "nesting dolls" on Onekotan Island.

And in 2022, the Landsat 8 satellite also spotted the iconic summit of Mount Vesuvius peeking through a gap in the clouds over Italy, just like Alaid.

A 2024 astronaut photo shows the icy surface of Pangong Lake breaking apart in the lofty Tibetan Plateau. The point where the ice meets the water almost perfectly matches a disputed border between China and India.

A 2020 astronaut photo shows the unique structure of Ol Doinyo Lengai, an active stratovolcano in Tanzania that was recently adorned with a bright white "ash cone." The explosive peak produces a rare type of lava that is unusually cool but travels remarkably quickly.

A 2010 satellite photo shows the point where a small lake bisects the snowy rim of an ancient glacier on Canada's Baffin Island. The rippling, snow-rimmed structure is the last remaining fragment of a colossal ice sheet that once covered large parts of North America.

#6429. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

#6428. Scientists Warn: The World Has Less Than Four Years of Carbon Budget Left

Solar power, wind energy, and electric vehicles are reshaping global emissions trends, but a new scientific assessment reveals that the world’s remaining carbon budget is shrinking at an alarming rate.

Global fossil fuel emissions are expected to fall slightly in 2026, but the world’s total carbon dioxide output is still projected to rise. A new assessment by the Global Carbon Project estimates that fossil CO2 emissions will decline by 0.4% to 38.2 billion metric tons (42.1 billion U.S. tons), partly because of expanding clean energy and disruptions linked to the Iran conflict.

However, increasing emissions from deforestation and other changes in land use are expected to push total global CO2 emissions to 43.3 billion metric tons (47.7 billion U.S. tons), up from 42.8 billion metric tons in 2025. The findings show that renewable energy is beginning to reshape global emissions trends, but its growth has not yet produced a sustained worldwide decline.

Oil is expected to account for much of the projected reduction in fossil fuel emissions. Global CO2 emissions from oil are forecast to drop by 1.9%, largely reflecting the energy shock associated with the Iran conflict, which has increased prices and constrained supplies. Natural gas emissions are expected to decrease by 0.3%, while coal emissions could rise by 0.6%. Emissions from international aviation and shipping are each projected to fall by 1%, with reduced activity in the Middle East contributing to the aviation decline.

“A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” said Professor Pierre Friedlingstein, director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter, who led the study. “The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies. While renewables and electric vehicles are increasingly offsetting growth in energy demand, further acceleration is needed if global emissions are to peak and enter a sustained decline.”

Glen Peters, Research Professor at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research, emphasized that temporary reductions should not be confused with lasting progress. “A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries, and electric vehicles are pushing emissions down in dozens of countries, and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions.”

Solar and wind power, together with electric vehicles, are increasingly limiting emissions despite rising energy demand. According to the assessment, these technologies are meeting or avoiding roughly two-thirds of the increase in global energy demand. Solar and wind generation alone are projected to prevent 4.6 billion metric tons (5.1 billion U.S. tons) of CO2 emissions in 2026, compared with 4.1 billion metric tons in 2025 and just 0.28 billion metric tons in 2010.

China is central to this transformation. Although it produces approximately 32% of global fossil fuel emissions, it also accounts for half of the emissions avoided worldwide through renewable energy and electric vehicles. China’s emissions are projected to decline by 0.9% in 2026, helped by lower oil consumption and continued renewable electricity expansion. Coal emissions, however, are expected to increase slightly by 0.3%. China also leads the world in carbon uptake from reforestation and afforestation (new forests).

“Clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions. Solar and wind power and electric vehicles are expanding rapidly, led by China. Countries on every continent are decreasing their emissions while growing their economies. A further acceleration could turn the tide on global emissions within a few years,” said Professor Corinne Le Quéré, Royal Society Research Professor at the University of East Anglia’s School of Environmental Sciences.

Emissions are projected to decline by 1.3% in the United States, primarily because coal consumption is falling after increasing in 2025 amid high natural gas prices and cold weather. The European Union is expected to record a 1.5% reduction, while Japan’s emissions could decrease by 1%. India is moving in the opposite direction, with emissions projected to rise by 4.4%, exceeding its average annual growth rate of 3.5% over the past decade. Emissions across the rest of the world are expected to decrease by 0.7%, largely because of reduced oil consumption.

An accompanying analysis, currently in press in a separate peer-reviewed journal, identifies a broader shift in the relationship between economic growth and carbon emissions. In 59 countries, emissions were lower in 2025 than in 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic, even as their economies expanded. Emissions growth has also slowed in regions where total emissions continue to rise, including China, India, and other emerging economies.

The decline in fossil fuel emissions is being offset by increasing carbon releases from land-use change (such as deforestation). These emissions are projected to reach 5.1 billion metric tons (5.6 billion U.S. tons) in 2026. The increase is linked partly to peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia, where drier conditions associated with El Niño have heightened fire risks. Nearly all peat fires are ignited by human activities.

Natural ecosystems also influence how much CO2 remains in the atmosphere. Forests, soils, and oceans absorb substantial amounts of carbon, acting as natural carbon sinks. The Global Carbon Budget reports that land-based carbon absorption has recovered after weakening sharply during the 2023 and 2024 El Niño event. However, the powerful El Niño developing in 2026 is expected to affect this natural carbon uptake over the coming year.

The latest assessment estimates that only 150 billion metric tons (165 billion U.S. tons) of CO2 can be emitted before cumulative emissions reach the level associated with 1.5°C (2.7°F) of global warming above preindustrial levels. At current emission rates, that remaining carbon budget amounts to less than four years. Meanwhile, atmospheric CO2 concentrations are projected to reach 427.7 parts per million in 2026, approximately 54% above preindustrial levels.

Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is another part of the challenge. Permanent deforestation released an average of approximately 3.8 billion metric tons (4.2 billion U.S. tons) of CO2 annually between 2016 and 2025. Reforestation and afforestation offset roughly half of those emissions. China, the European Union, and the United States account for the largest combined removals through forest restoration and expansion, while deforestation outweighs these gains in countries including Brazil, Russia, and Indonesia. Technologies designed to remove atmospheric CO2 remain limited, currently capturing less than the amount released by fossil fuels in just 30 minutes.

“Alongside reducing emissions, we need to scale up CO2 removal to reach greenhouse gas neutrality. Afforestation and reforestation already remove substantial amounts of CO2, but these gains are still more than offset by emissions from deforestation, and novel carbon removal remains very limited. We need to act on all these fronts now,” said Professor Julia Pongratz of Ludwig-Maximilian-University Munich.

Despite continued increases in total emissions, their long-term growth rate has slowed substantially. Global CO2 emissions rose by an average of 0.3% annually over the past decade, compared with 1.7% annually during the preceding decade. The accompanying analysis projects that between now and the end of 2028, additional solar and wind generation and electric vehicles could prevent emissions equivalent to 64% to 79% of those associated with rising energy demand. Electric vehicles are becoming increasingly influential, although only about 10% of the global passenger car fleet was electrified in 2025 (or 6% excluding hybrids).

The researchers conclude that continued deployment of clean technologies could bring the first sustained global decline in CO2 emissions within reach. However, achieving that outcome depends on maintaining and accelerating their expansion rather than relying on temporary reductions caused by economic or geopolitical disruptions. As the authors write, “If further acceleration of clean technology deployment can be supported through time, a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away.”

Reference: “Global Carbon Budget 2026” by Pierre Friedlingstein, Michael O’Sullivan, Robbie M. Andrew, Judith Hauck, Matthew W. Jones, Peter Landschützer, Corinne Le Quéré, Hongmei Li, Ingrid T. #6426. Scientists Discover New Form of Prostate Cancer

Researchers at the University of British Columbia have identified a previously unrecognized form of hereditary prostate cancer linked to a rare genetic mutation that can lead to aggressive disease at relatively young ages. The discovery could help doctors identify families with an inherited cancer risk and introduce earlier screening, potentially detecting tumors before they spread.

The new study, published in Cancer Discovery, connects this form of hereditary prostate cancer to inherited mutations in a gene called CDK12. After analyzing genetic data from more than 4,500 people with aggressive prostate cancer, researchers identified five unrelated men carrying these mutations. All five developed metastatic prostate cancer between ages 44 and 62.

Scientists previously believed that harmful CDK12 mutations developed spontaneously within tumor cells rather than being inherited from a parent. To investigate whether inherited mutations were responsible for the cancers, researchers examined the patients’ tumors for a distinctive pattern of genetic changes associated with CDK12 dysfunction.

“The tumors provided us with a genetic signature that pointed directly back to CDK12,” said lead author Dr. Sofie Tolmeijer, a postdoctoral fellow in the Wyatt lab. “It gave us compelling evidence that these inherited mutations were playing a direct role in causing their cancer.”

“What’s striking is that every patient we identified with this inherited mutation had already developed metastatic disease by the time they were diagnosed,” said senior author Dr. Alexander Wyatt, associate professor of urologic sciences at UBC and UBC President’s Excellence Chair in Precision Oncology. “The opportunity now is to identify these families earlier and give people the chance to benefit from enhanced screening, when there are still curative treatment options.”

Approximately 5 to 10 percent of cancers are associated with inherited genetic mutations, rather than changes that accumulate during a person’s lifetime. Among the best-known examples are BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations, which increase the risk of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and prostate cancers. Genetic testing for these mutations already helps guide cancer screening and preventive care.

Inherited CDK12 mutations appear considerably rarer. The researchers estimate that they occur in approximately one in 1,000 people with aggressive prostate cancer, potentially affecting hundreds of families worldwide. Identifying a carrier could allow relatives to undergo genetic testing and determine whether they share the mutation.

“While this mutation is extremely rare, the discovery could be lifesaving for the families who carry it,” said Dr. Tolmeijer. “Finding one person with an inherited mutation gives us the opportunity to identify other family members at risk and help them take action before cancer develops or spreads.”

The research team recommends considering CDK12 for inclusion in standard hereditary prostate cancer testing panels. Unlike genetic discoveries that require new diagnostic methods, CDK12 mutations can already be detected using existing clinical technology, potentially making expanded testing faster and less expensive to implement.

“One of the most exciting aspects of this discovery is that we already have the technology needed to act on it,” said Dr. Wyatt, who is also a senior research scientist at the Vancouver Prostate Centre and senior scientist at BC Cancer. “Adding CDK12 to existing genetic tests is relatively straightforward, which means this discovery could move from the research lab into clinical care much more quickly.”

The findings also raise questions about whether inherited CDK12 mutations contribute to ovarian cancer. Several affected men had family histories of ovarian cancer, and researchers identified an additional person with ovarian cancer who carried an inherited CDK12 mutation. That person’s tumor displayed the same characteristic genetic changes associated with CDK12 dysfunction. Further research is needed to establish whether the mutation increases ovarian cancer risk.

“With the right genetic testing and screening programs, we envision a future where no one who inherits one of these mutations dies from cancer,” said Dr. Wyatt.

Reference: “Germline CDK12 Variants in Aggressive Prostate Cancer” by Sofie H. Julie Elie, an ethologist at the University of California, Berkeley, tells Live Science's Kenna Hughes-Castleberry about using AI to decode the vocalizations of zebra finches.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Bird calls are far more than pleasant sounds in nature. They are complex forms of communication that can reveal how birds think, learn, cooperate and respond to their surroundings. From intricate songs used to attract mates to alarm calls that warn others of danger, vocalizations offer valuable clues about avian intelligence and social organization.

Julie Elie is an animal behavior researcher and associate project scientist at the University of California, Berkeley. She recently won the 2026 Coller Dolittle Challenge for Two-Way Interspecies Communication for her work in studying and deciphering zebra finch communication.

For more than a decade, Elie observed the social behavior of birds, recording thousands of sounds and using machine learning combined with behavioral experiments to decode specific calls.

In this interview, Elie discusses how zebra finches learn and use vocalizations, what their calls reveal about intelligence and social relationships and how artificial intelligence (AI) contributed to decoding birdsong.

Dr Julie Elie is a computational neuroethologist who studies how social animals communicate. Her research combines behavioral experiments, neuroscience, and computational tools to reveal how animals produce communication sounds, what information they transmit in their vocalizations and how they perceive the meaning of vocalizations.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: What made you study birds and birdsong?

Julie Elie: The beginning of my work with birds dates from my Ph.D. I've always been super interested in animal behavior in general. But I think as a young person, I was more attracted by animals that we relate more easily to, which are mammals, right? Dogs, cats, horses.

I wanted to do a Ph.D. on animal behavior and, more specifically, on relationships between animals. I was interested in how animals interact with each other and what kind of social organization they establish.

[Someone suggested I] work on the zebra finch, and I said, "OK, I've never taken the time to really observe birds very well; might as well start now."

I realized that it's difficult to observe birds because they're not close to you. They can fly wherever they want. When you are out and about in town, in the countryside, and you see birds, they're here, and then they're gone. You don't get to see a lot of their vocal interactions or a lot of their social interactions.

So here I was, studying the zebra finch in cages where they were fully interacting with each other. And the question was, what kind of social organization do they have?

I realized quickly that they were not doing a dominance hierarchy [which was previously thought to be the case], but instead, the most important thing in their life was their partner. They were doing pair bonds, and that's the core of their social organization, [with] males and females pairing for life.

Studying birdsong can help researchers like Elie better understand how the birds navigate their complex environments.

KHC: Why is it important to study birdsong, and what can it teach us about intelligence and behavior?

JE: A level of complexity we were trying to understand was, what are the neural mechanisms that enable those birds to do this process of listening to something and copying it, and reproducing it, and doing a comparison between what they're producing and what they're hearing?

The zebra finch is a just-right middle ground level of cognitive ability that is interesting, where you see this pattern of copying vocalization and producing it. But you can look through the avian kingdom, and some species show more complex behaviors.

We know that there are some species that are able to not only imitate their own vocalizations from their own species, their dad, but they're able to copy other species. So, here in California, for instance, a mockingbird is a bird that is really known to be able to reproduce a bunch of different sounds and is actually incorporating this in their vocalizations.

Parrots are also well known for that because we have them as pets, and they're able to reproduce our own vocalizations as humans. This is kind of crazy, when you think about it, because they don't have the same vocal tract as we do. It's smaller, and they have a different system. I think a high cognitive level is when an animal is able to reproduce a sound that is not in their "native language," let's say, and use it for a goal. We do see this in parrots ‪—‬ they're able to ask you for something or even ask the dog to shut up sometimes, which is interesting. They're able to really use those vocalizations, such as "This is not mine, but I communicate with another species this way."

It shows you how smart they can be, and by studying vocal communication in animals, we are getting a window of what cognitive abilities they have and how the usage reveals their level of smartness.

KHC: Could you walk me through how you ended up decoding bird vocalizations?

JE: I spent countless hours observing zebra finches, and I realized that I could progressively do a match between the social context and the acoustic characteristics of the sound produced. I could recognize these sounds and understand what they "mean."

It's like at home with your cat or dog: Within a couple of months, you figure out every time the cat is doing this kind of sound —‬ "meow" — ‬it means he wants to get out or he's hungry, or he wants to cuddle. Same thing with the dog. It's the same process, but instead of doing this with cats or dogs, I did this with birds and constituted the first acoustic dictionary of zebra finch calls.

However, how do you know you are correct? That you correctly identified the sounds that correspond to the "words" in that species?

Pet owners can often differentiate between different vocalizations in their pets, such as different meowing noises for their cat.

I thought that the best confirmation of whether I was right or not could only come from the zebra finches themselves. Up to now, nobody had found a way to systematically go through the vocal repertoire of an animal and confirm if each identified call type was indeed perceived as a word in that species' language.

To achieve this somewhat impossible discussion with a bird, we designed an operant conditioning experiment where the bird is asked to classify vocalizations that were previously recorded from other zebra finches. The game is simple and relies on two rules. The first one is that every day, only the recordings corresponding to one call type are rewarded by seeds, while the recordings from the other call types in the repertoire are not rewarded. The second rule is that the bird can interrupt recordings and skip to the next one whenever they want, like how you skip through songs on your favorite music app.

The bird is placed in a cage that has a button or a little infrared sensor that it can activate with its beak. Each time it does so, the recording of a vocalization randomly drawn from the library of call types is played. Four out of five times, birds trigger the playback of a call type that will not give them access to seeds. Because they are slightly food deprived, they only really want to listen to the rewarded playback, so they interrupt the nonrewarded calls and only listen for the calls that are going to be rewarded.

Every day, the bird has to find out which call type or "word" is rewarded. They usually figure it out pretty rapidly and then start interrupting the playback of all the other call types. Using this task, we could test a different call type every dayIf they had not been able to do it, it would tell us that the call type we had identified was in fact not existing in their language. If they were able to do it ‪—‬ and spoiler alert, they were! ‪—‬ it meant that we had correctly identified that call type.

The birds told us yes, basically —‬ the organization that you're proposing is correct.

But then we made a surprising discovery. We noticed that birds were making some rare and systematic mistakes. We wondered if these mistakes were coming from the acoustic similarity of the call types — how you might mistake, for instance, the word "glove" for "love" or "hurt" for "heart." Or if they were coming from the semantic similarity of the call types — you could maybe mistake "love" for "heart" if you are remembering about the general meaning of the rewarded word today, which is "love.".

In that last case, it would mean that birds truly have an understanding of their call types' meaning. We found out that birds' errors could be better explained by the meaning [the semantic similarity] of the call types. That is a big discovery in the field of animal communication.

I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird.

KHC: Do you think we are headed toward actually being able to communicate with birds, or do you think it's more that we're still testing the waters and we still need to learn the rest of the language before we get there?

JE: When we say "talking with birds," I think we need to understand that it's not going to be a language. Right now, I am studying the zebra finch; it doesn't mean that I would be able to communicate with a crow once I have a repertoire. So there's this component of when we talk about birds, there are many different species.

I think there's more traction in this particular part of the animal kingdom than in other parts, just because birds are really talkative. Birds use a lot of their vocalizations to communicate with each other. So because of that, I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird, just because they are very talkative.

For now, I found all those words. But we need to understand how those words are [strung] together. So it's not necessarily the case that we need to understand the rules of the dynamic exchanges between individuals or how fast you're responding, but how you are responding and whether that makes sense or not.

They [also] have [body] postures. They have specific displays at the same time they're producing the vocalizations. And if we really want to achieve full communication with another species, we need to get to that level.

It's not tomorrow for sure, it's probably not next year, but I think in the range of 10 years we should get there. Especially with how fast the domains of AI and robotics are. I have some hope that we should be able to get to that point.

KHC: Is there one takeaway you would want our readers to know about your work?

JE: Just one. The most important thing for readers that are not specifically scientists is to realize that, by studying animal behavior more generally, researchers are discovering the intelligence of animals. This is opening our eyes to other species and realizing that we're not the only species that is intelligent on this planet.

This is a lesson to us as another species on this planet, that we are not the only ones that are smart and we need to take this into account in how we are evolving.

We need to realize how we're affecting them and realize that they also have their own internal lives, and maybe we should start to respect them a little bit more.

Editor's note: Some of this interview was conducted via email as part of a follow-up conversation. The interview has been edited lightly for clarity and length.

#6423. Blood Vessel Function Improved Just 60 Minutes After Taking This Anti-Aging Supplement

Blood vessel function improved within an hour of a supplement’s first dose in a small human trial, though lasting protection against cardiovascular disease remains unproven.

What if protecting the heart and blood vessels requires more than treating traditional risk factors such as high blood pressure and cholesterol?

Cardiovascular disease remains the world’s leading cause of death, and researchers at the University of Surrey are exploring whether targeting the biology of aging could help protect the heart and blood vessels. In a small trial, they tested a nutritional supplement designed to address several aging-related processes at once, finding improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure over six months.

The randomized controlled trial enrolled 61 participants, with 33 taking NOVOS Core and 28 receiving a placebo once daily for six months. Researchers investigated whether combining these substances could improve cardiovascular health by influencing multiple aging-related pathways simultaneously.

The supplement combines 12 ingredients selected to target biological processes associated with aging. These include glycine, magnesium malate, calcium alpha-ketoglutarate, glucosamine sulfate, vitamin C, L-theanine, hyaluronic acid, and small amounts of lithium, along with plant-derived compounds such as fisetin, pterostilbene, Rhodiola rosea extract, and ginger extract.

Professor Christian Heiss, Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Surrey, said: “Biological aging is not driven by one pathway, but by a number of interacting molecular and cellular processes. The idea behind this study was to ask whether addressing several of these processes at the same time via a nutritional supplement could produce measurable effects on cardiovascular health biomarkers.

“As a first step, we looked at established biomarkers of vascular health, such as blood pressure and cholesterol levels, rather than clinical outcomes. We found favorable changes in endothelial function, arterial stiffness, and systolic blood pressure after six months. These findings are encouraging. We now need larger studies to understand the mechanisms involved and, importantly, whether these changes translate into longer-term health benefits.”

Researchers measured flow-mediated dilation, or how readily an artery widens as blood flow increases. This reveals how well its inner lining, the endothelium, works to regulate vessel width and blood clotting. Dilation improved in the supplement group compared with the placebo group after six months. An improvement also appeared just one hour after the first dose, while placebo readings remained largely unchanged.

Arteries were also less stiff in the supplement group. Researchers assessed this using pulse wave velocity, the speed at which a pressure wave travels through arteries. Slower waves indicate more flexible arteries, and the adjusted difference between groups was 1.18 meters per second after six months.

Systolic blood pressure, the pressure when the heart contracts, was an adjusted 6.1 mmHg lower in the supplement group than in the placebo group at six months. A difference was also observed one hour after the first dose. Estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk decreased modestly, largely reflecting the blood pressure difference.

Previous large studies have associated a sustained 5 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure with approximately 10 percent fewer major cardiovascular events. The Surrey trial measured markers associated with risk and was not designed to determine whether participants experienced fewer such events.

Diogo Barardo, PhD, Director of R&D at NOVOS and a geroscientist, a scientist specializing in the biology of aging, said:

“When we began developing NOVOS Core in 2019, our hypothesis was that simultaneously targeting all the hallmarks of aging, the fundamental biological processes underlying aging and age-related diseases, could produce measurable improvements in the organs and systems affected by aging.

“The STAMINA results provide encouraging clinical evidence consistent with that hypothesis, demonstrating improvements across three measures of cardiovascular function, particularly meaningful given that cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death worldwide.”

Blood tests showed no significant changes in cholesterol or other blood lipids, suggesting that lipid lowering did not explain the improvements in blood vessel measures.

Professor Juliet Wright, Founding Dean of the School of Medicine at the University of Surrey, said:

“This study is a good example of how ideas emerging from the biology of aging can be tested rigorously in people. The findings provide an interesting proof of concept, but the important next step is to understand the underlying biology and establish whether changes in cardiovascular biomarkers translate into meaningful longer-term health benefits.”

Reference: “Acute and 6-month vascular effects of a multi-component nutritional supplement: a randomized controlled trial” by Charles Piercy, Jenny Harris, Kenza Sackho, Paola Campagnolo, Diogo Barardo, Ben Creagh-Brown and Christian Heiss, 4 November 2026, European Heart Journal Open. DOI: 10.1093/ehjopen/oeag157

The investigator-initiated study was supported by NOVOS Labs through provision of the study supplement known as NOVOS Core and matching control and an unrestricted contribution towards research costs. NOVOS Labs had no role in study design, collection, or primary interpretation of the data, or the decision to publish.

#6422. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

W. Xin et al. Overcoming environmental constraints: octopus uses 3-step or 4-step strategies to squeeze through small holes. Journal of Experimental Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1242/jeb.252825

#6420. Scientists Warn of a Disturbing Rise in Vitamin K Deficiency Among American Newborns

Only about one in five infants diagnosed with vitamin K-related bleeding had received the shot, U.S. health records show.

Babies are born with little vitamin K, leaving them vulnerable to bleeding that can cause permanent brain damage or death. A single shot helps protect against that danger. The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended one dose injected into a muscle for newborns since 1961, and a growing number of American parents are choosing to skip it.

That trend has coincided with a sharp rise in diagnoses of vitamin K deficiency (VKD) and vitamin-K-deficient bleeding (VKDB). A nationwide study found that their rates increased by 216% and 347%, respectively, between 2017 and 2025, while the percentage of newborns receiving injectable vitamin K fell from 97.7% to 95.0%. The findings were published on November 5, 2026, in JAMA Pediatrics.

Vitamin K activates specialized proteins needed for normal blood clotting. Newborns receive too little through the placenta, absorb it poorly through their digestive systems, and get little from breast milk. The injection addresses a deficiency at a time when its consequences can be severe.

Classical VKD occurs between 2 days and 1 week after birth and causes bruising and bleeding from the umbilicus, or belly button. Late VKD, which occurs between 1 week and 6 months of age, carries a 30% to 60% risk of intracranial hemorrhage, or bleeding inside the skull. That bleeding can lead to seizures, permanent brain damage, or death.

Refusal of the shot has increased over the past decade. Previous studies found that the proportion of newborns who did not receive intramuscular vitamin K rose from 2.9% in 2017 to 5.2% in 2024.

To investigate the consequences of that trend, Elizabeth Wolf, M.D., MPH, led the new nationwide study. Wolf is a pediatrician at Children’s Hospital of Richmond at VCU and an associate professor in the Department of Pediatrics at Virginia Commonwealth University School of Medicine.

The researchers analyzed de-identified electronic health records from a large national database covering health systems across the United States. Their analysis included more than 11 million infants aged 0 to 6 months who were born at 35 weeks’ gestation or later and received care between 2017 and 2025.

Only 40% of infants diagnosed with VKD and about 19% of those diagnosed with VKDB had received vitamin K shots. About 7% of infants with VKD and 2% of those with VKDB also had a diagnosis of intracranial or intracerebral hemorrhage, meaning bleeding inside the skull or within the brain tissue itself.

“We knew from prior studies that vitamin K refusal had been increasing in the U.S., and we wanted to learn if there were any real-life consequences of this trend,” Wolf said. “We found that the answer is undeniably yes, with the rates of VKD and VKDB multiplying over the course of our study.”

The researchers caution that the simultaneous decline in injections and increase in diagnoses does not prove causation. Wolf considers other explanations unlikely, however, because behaviors and diseases that increase the risk of VKD remained constant or decreased during the study period.

The study’s co-authors included Steven Woolf, M.D., director emeritus of the VCU Center on Society and Health and a professor in VCU School of Medicine’s Department of Family Medicine, Evan French, MS, of VCU’s C. Kenneth and Dianne Wright Center for Clinical and Translational Research, and Darya Shokouhi Niaki, Pharm.D., of the VCU School of Public Health’s Department of Biostatistics.

Wolf connected the findings to growing mistrust of doctors and public health professionals.

“Similar to the recent measles outbreaks, we are seeing the real-world implications of growing mistrust of doctors and public health professionals. We need clear messaging from all levels of public health about the benefits of vitamin K administration for newborns.”

Like childhood vaccines, the researchers say, vitamin K has been “a victim of its own success,” with many parents unaware that refusing the shot can have serious lifelong consequences. Wolf says more research is needed to determine how best to communicate the seriousness of vitamin K deficiency and encourage use of the medication in newborns.

“We should continue to follow these trends moving forward since the rates of vitamin K deficiency and vitamin-K-deficient bleeding may continue to rise if vitamin K refusal keeps increasing. We need to better understand why parents are refusing vitamin K and what can be done to improve the uptake of this important medication,” Wolf said.

Reference: “Vitamin K Deficiency and Associated Bleeding in Infants” by Elizabeth R. Wolf, Evan French, Darya Shokouhi Niaki and Steven H. Woolf, 5 November 2026, JAMA Pediatrics. DOI: 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2026.5794

#6419. ZWO Seestar S30 Plus review

We tested the brand-new ZWO Seestar S30 Plus, an all-in-one smart telescope for beginners and hobbyists that makes astrophotography accessible to everyone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus. The image quality is great, it's easy to use, and it's compact and lightweight enough to take it anywhere. It's not quite as good as the more expensive S30 Pro, but it's a nice middle-ground option between the S30 and the S30 Pro that gives you a lot of features for the money.

Seestar app is reliable and easy to navigate

All-in-one workflow from shooting to sharing

2K image quality is better than we expected

Editing controls could be a little more responsive

Not suitable for smaller planetary nebulas

Why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you. Find out more about how we test.

ZWO has just released the newest member of its smart telescope range: the Seestar S30 Plus. This all-in-one smart telescope is designed for beginners and hobbyists who want an affordable way into astrophotography that won't leave you scratching your head, and lets you capture, process and share your images in one simple workflow. It sits between the Seestar S30 and S30 Pro, and is priced at $499 for its release.

With 2K image quality, a light pollution filter and a user-friendly interface, it's a smart telescope that anyone can enjoy, regardless of your experience level, and regardless of whether you're shooting from your city balcony or a dark sky site. Like the other models, it uses dual cameras to capture a wide range of subjects, including deep-sky objects with the telephoto camera, and constellations, star trails and the Milky Way with the wide-angle camera. It's lightweight and easy to travel with, and it even comes with a separate solar filter for solar imaging and eclipse time-lapses.

We got our hands on an advance copy to test ahead of its release, so we put it through its paces on several different celestial subjects.

The Seestar S30 Plus is one of the smallest, most compact smart telescopes on the market, weighing just 3.63 pounds (1.65 kg) and measuring 8.3 x 5.5 x 3.2 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm). Its sleek, matte white design looks identical to the other Seestar models (we compared it to our S30 Pro), except for the branding on the unit itself.

It comes in a padded soft carry case and includes a small tripod (although we always prefer to use our own), a solar filter, a 40-inch (1 meter) USB-A to USB-C charging cable, a removable shoulder strap for the carry case, and a quick-start guide. With its accessories and case, the whole setup weighs 4.89 pounds (2.22 kg).

On the unit itself, you'll find just one button, which powers it on, plus the USB-C port on the side. Super simple, although we'd have liked the USB-C port to be covered to prevent moisture or dust from getting in.

It comes with a carry case, strap, USB-C cable and solar filter.

The set-up process couldn't be easier. When you turn the telescope on, you'll hear a double beep and see the power button light up alongside the red dots on the black screen to indicate the battery level. Four dots mean the battery is full. The telescope will tell you when it's ready to connect, at which point you can sync it up to the app on your smartphone or tablet. To turn it off, you just select "Shutdown" in the app, which closes the arm and turns the unit off.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It also features an anti-dew heater, which we've found works quite well in mild to moderate humidity. On a couple of our shoots, we noticed a tiny bit of condensation forming on the unit when the humidity was higher, so we wouldn't feel confident leaving it unsupervised for long periods on a particularly dewy evening. (We used the Clear Outside app to monitor the humidity levels.)

The Seestar App is user-friendly and easy to navigate, with just the right amount of controls: you have plenty of options to choose from but it doesn’t become overwhelming. The main Seestar page is where you'll likely spend most of your time, as this is where you can search for celestial objects to shoot, access your album, plan a shoot and read up on what objects Seestar recommends based on your time and location.

The Stargazing section is where you can select or search for the subject you want to shoot. You can use the search function to find a specific target or browse Tonight's Best, and you can also search through different types of subjects like galaxies, nebulas, clusters and more. From here, you can also select planets, track comets and photograph constellations using the wide camera.

Click on a subject and the app will display information about it, including its current altitude and coordinates, which help determine what time is best to shoot that particular object. It automatically applies the appropriate filters and settings, but you can override these if you want to.

There's very little to complain about when it comes to using the app. It has lots of information for beginners, so you don't need a ton of knowledge about the night sky, and everything is fairly self-explanatory. There were a couple of occasions when it failed to calibrate itself (for example, when we tried to locate the Pleiades, which had just risen above a tree), and other times when we chose a new target and it slewed the long way round instead of only having to move slightly. But otherwise, the app worked well.

The AI Enhance section has some good editing tools to bring out the best from your photos. You can reduce the stars, adjust the brightness, contrast, saturation and RGB curves, apply denoise and eliminate any satellite trails — although we'd love a dehaze slider to bring out some of the fainter nebulosity of certain objects. The sliders could do with being a little more responsive, especially the RGB curves, but overall, it does a pretty good job of editing your pictures to get a pleasing result.

We had about 10 days to test our review unit before its release, so we could only capture as much as the weather permitted in that time. We'll add more images to this review over the coming weeks. All our tests were conducted from our backyard in a Bortle 4 region, and captured before moonrise to eliminate as much light pollution as possible. Due to these time constraints, we aimed to capture our images for a total of 60 minutes each, although we'd have ideally aimed for longer in some cases.

Now for the fun part — the images. The Seestar S30 Plus has a focal length of 160mm, which is advantageous for capturing large subjects like the Andromeda Galaxy, the North America Nebula and the Pleiades. Large emission nebulas are where it really shines; however, the focal length is too short to capture smaller apparent objects.

For this review, we aimed to capture as many different types of objects as possible. All our images were edited in the Seestar app with, in some cases, a few minor tweaks in Lightroom. You also have the option to download the individual files to your computer to process them yourself in dedicated astrophotography software, which is advantageous if you're a more experienced user.

Everyone's favorite star cluster, the Pleiades, was one of the first targets we wanted to capture. We could see the faint blue nebulosity after as little as 15 minutes of integration time, and it only improved over time. After 60 minutes, we had a really nice image and could easily bring out the blue haze via the editing tools in the app. However, we got a much more impressive result after tweaking our image a little further in Lightroom, bringing out even more haze and reflective dust.

The Andromeda Galaxy is a perfect target for the Seestar S30 Plus. It takes up a large portion of the frame, and with long integration times, it can reveal beautiful details in the faint outer arms. We shot for around an hour in our tests due to weather and time constraints, but we still got an impressive image. As we approached 60 minutes, there was a lot of cloud cover, and we noticed it struggling to stack images toward the end of the session, so we stopped the integration at 57 minutes.

Andromeda is certainly going to be the most impressive galaxy for the Seestar visually, as most others will appear smaller in the frame and will need longer integration, so make sure you have a clear, dark night for it.

Large emission nebulas are where the Seestar S30 Plus thrives, and the North America Nebula is a great target. It covers the whole field of view, and the red hydrogen gas easily comes to the forefront of the image.

The Eastern Veil Nebula is another lovely target where you can bring out the beautiful red and turquoise hues in as little as 15 minutes, but longer integration times will yield brighter, more colorful results.

Planetary nebulas are where you will see the limitations of the Seestar's 160mm focal length. Most planetary nebulas have a very small apparent size — we've previously captured the Dumbbell Nebula and Cocoon Nebula with our S30 Pro, and they were a tiny dot in the middle of the screen. We tried the Helix Nebula, and even though it's one of the largest apparent planetary nebulas, it's still fairly small on the Seestar S30 Plus. You can still get a decent image of it, but if you want to focus on imaging planetary nebulas, you'll need a bigger scope. Because it was very low in the sky and there was some interfering cloud, we stopped integration at 27 minutes.

The Seestar S30 Plus is an affordable entry point into deep-sky astrophotography without the confusing settings and expensive setup. It's ideal for beginners, although more experienced users will likely want to upgrade to the superior image quality and extra features of the S30 Pro.

Still, for under $500, we can't complain. Not only is the Seestar S30 Plus easy to navigate and use, but it teaches you about space in a fun and interactive way, and you don't need to spend hours stacking individual frames on your computer to process — although you still can do that if you want more control over your editing.

If you can stretch your budget, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade. It produces 4K images and offers more pro-level features.

To see deeper into space, the Seestar S50 Pro has a longer focal length of 260mm and a larger 50mm aperture, making it better for smaller apparent objects.

If the imaging aspect doesn't interest you, the Celestron StarSense Explorer range of telescopes connects to your phone to guide you around the sky, but you observe the cosmos through an eyepiece instead of capturing it on your phone.

Read our full Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ review

Kimberley Lane, E-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, reviewing camera gear from Sony, Canon, OM System and more. With over 6 years of photography experience, her skills span across landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. She has also contributed to our sister site Space.com and Tech Radar, and she regularly uses binoculars and telescopes to stargaze in the dark skies of South Wales.

#6416. Ancient Tomb Reveals That People Were Getting High on Cannabis 2,800 Years Ago

The oldest directly dated evidence of intoxicating cannabis use comes from a Scythian tomb, suggesting the plant’s mind-altering effects had a place in ancient burial rituals.

About 1,000 cannabis seeds recovered from a princely tomb in southern Siberia could not, on their own, tell archaeologists whether anyone had used the plant to get high. Cannabis, one of today’s most commonly used psychoactive plants, has also supplied oil, fiber, and medicine, and its flowers, leaves, and resins rarely survive to help distinguish among prehistoric uses.

The tomb, in the South Siberian Republic of Tyva, belonged to high-ranking members of Scythian society, a horse-riding culture of the Eurasian steppe. Researchers investigating the burial found another source of evidence in preserved human hair from its central chamber.

Dr. Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the University of Bern’s Institute of Archaeological Sciences and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Jena, Germany, led the international research team and is the lead author of the study, published in Science. “The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties,” he says.

By directly radiocarbon dating six seeds and combining those measurements with other dating results, the researchers determined that the seeds were placed in the grave in the early eighth century B.C. The findings provide what is currently the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence of cannabis use for its intoxicating properties. “The seeds show that cannabis played an important role in the rituals surrounding the burial,” says Caspari.

In an earlier publication, the team described the remains of 18 horses that had once been arranged on the burial mound. Several dozen additional horse sacrifices and scattered human bones have since come to light. “In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well,” says Caspari.

To investigate whether cannabis compounds had entered the bodies of people buried there, the researchers analyzed the hair using high-resolution mass spectrometry and other methods. Mass spectrometry helps distinguish compounds by the mass and electrical charge of their molecules or fragments. Several hair samples produced clear signals consistent with cannabinol, or CBN, a compound that can form through the oxidation of tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, the main intoxicating compound in cannabis. The team also detected weak signals whose masses were consistent with THC.

“This study is particularly insightful because it combines the analysis of plant remains with molecular traces in the human body,” says Caspari.

The researchers interpret the hair results as evidence of cannabis use, although the analyses cannot reliably establish how much was consumed or determine with certainty how its active compounds entered the body, such as through inhalation or ingestion. Later archaeological sites in Central Asia have yielded chemical residues of cannabinoids, compounds found in cannabis, in vessels and on heated stones that clearly indicate inhalation. The Tyva hair samples do not establish a particular method of consumption.

The recovered seeds likely came from wild plants, and the findings do not reveal how much THC those plants contained. It also remains unclear whether people specifically cultivated cannabis for its psychoactive properties or selected or cultivated plants for higher levels of active compounds.

The team is continuing its investigation. “We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples,” says Caspari. “DNA preservation is excellent in this case. This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of this crop soon.”

Reference: “Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago” by Gino Caspari, Timur Sadykov, Daria Fomicheva, Jegor Blochin, Dominic Armbruster, Oliver Happel, Natalia Ryabogina, Kseniia Boxleitner and Robert Spengler, 5 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aeg3800

#6415. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

#6412. Stonehenge’s Mysterious Six-Ton Stone Has Scientists Searching Across Britain

Stonehenge’s six-ton Altar Stone has led scientists from Wales to Scotland, yet even its most detailed geological examination has failed to reveal where it came from.

Scientists have spent more than a century trying to determine where Stonehenge’s six-ton Altar Stone came from. Once thought to originate in Wales, the massive sandstone slab has since been traced geologically to northeast Scotland, but its exact source remains unknown. Now, the most comprehensive geological investigation yet has ruled out several proposed locations and provided new clues to guide the search.

Published in the Journal of the Geological Society, the study examined the stone’s mineral composition, chemistry, and other geological characteristics. Measuring 4.9 meters (16 feet) long and weighing about six metric tons (6.6 US tons), the Altar Stone could offer important insights into how prehistoric people transported massive stones across Britain thousands of years ago.

The latest investigation brought together observations of the Altar Stone itself and detailed examinations of fragments held in museum collections. By comparing its structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic characteristics, the team assembled a set of identifying features that potential sources must match.

No location examined so far in northeast Scotland’s Orcadian Basin has met all those criteria. That leaves the stone’s birthplace unresolved but gives future fieldwork a clearer target. Study leader Duncan Pirrie, emeritus professor at the University of South Wales, said:

“This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone’s composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer.”

The findings build on earlier work that redirected the search away from Wales. Richard Bevins, honorary professor in Aberystwyth University’s Department of Geography and Earth Sciences, said:

“For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge’s most enduring mysteries.”

Nick Pearce, emeritus professor of geochemistry in the same department at Aberystwyth University, emphasized the value of eliminating candidates: “In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago.”

Stonehenge took shape through several construction phases between around 3000 and 1600 BC. Moving its stones across great distances was part of that achievement: the smaller bluestones traveled approximately 225 kilometers (140 miles) from west Wales.

Establishing where the Altar Stone began would give researchers a crucial geographical anchor for investigating how it reached the monument. The researchers hope that fingerprint will ultimately lead them to the source and shed new light on the effort behind one of prehistory’s most remarkable engineering achievements.

Reference: “Searching for the origin of the Stonehenge Altar Stone: new sedimentological, petrographical, mineralogical, geochemical and isotopic constraints” by Duncan Pirrie, Richard E.
