A fresh look at Einstein's equations suggests that gravity can sometimes snap and reconnect, similar to magnetic field lines on the sun. The findings hint at a new way that gravity and matter can trade energy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Magnetic reconnection — the process behind the sun's most violent outbursts — may have a counterpart in gravity.

According to a new theoretical study, sheet-like structures in the gravitational field can break apart and reconnect in new arrangements, much like the magnetic field lines that unleash solar flares.

Built entirely on Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, the study spells out when this "gravitational reconnection" can happen. It also offers a way to measure how fast the theoretical reconnection proceeds, and suggests a change to how gravity and matter trade energy. The process could even play a role in black hole collisions, the researchers suggest.

Magnetic field lines are normally "frozen" into plasma — the hot, electrically charged gas that makes up stars — and carried along wherever it flows. The lines can be stretched and twisted, but not cut. Where this rule breaks down, they can snap and rejoin in a process called magnetic reconnection, releasing pent-up energy in explosive bursts such as solar flares.

"In plasma physics, reconnection has become an essential part of our understanding of how magnetic fields reorganize and exchange energy with matter," Luca Comisso, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, told Live Science via email. "Could something similar be true for gravity?"

"Gravity and magnetism describe very different aspects of nature, so there's no obvious reason to expect them to behave alike," Comisso said. "But when we express Einstein's equations in a particular mathematical form, some of the same principles that govern magnetic fields also emerge in gravity. We wanted to understand whether those similarities extended to reconnection itself."

Comisso and study co-author Felipe Asenjo, a physicist at Adolfo Ibáñez University in Chile, used a mathematical framework known as the tetrad formulation. "Einstein's theory describes gravity through the geometry of space-time," Comisso explained. But in the tetrad formulation, "certain aspects of gravity can be expressed through quantities resembling electric and magnetic fields."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a prior study published in the journal Physical Review Letters earlier this year, the researchers applied this framework to gravity. That study suggested that gravitational fields can form two-dimensional structures called gravitational field sheets. Of the sheets' two dimensions, one stretches through space and the other through time — so each sheet is the trail a line leaves as time passes. A snapshot at any instant therefore catches each sheet as a line, akin to the field lines drawn around a magnet. And, like magnetic field lines frozen into a plasma, "under certain conditions, these sheets evolve without breaking or changing how they are connected," Comisso said.

An illustration depicting the sun’s magnetic field lines over an image taken by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. When magnetic loops get stretched to their limit, they snap and reconnect, triggering solar flares.

In the new study, published Oct. 28 in the journal Physical Review D, the researchers found that this is not always the case. "Gravitational field sheets can break and reconnect in a different arrangement, much like magnetic field lines do in plasmas," Comisso said.

The researchers showed that breaking the frozen-in rule doesn't, by itself, guarantee reconnection. Sometimes, the sheets merely slip relative to the flow that carries them, staying intact because they remain frozen into a different flow. Genuine reconnection happens only when no such alternative flow exists.

"We also derived equations describing how quickly this reconnection can occur and how it can affect the transfer of energy and momentum," Comisso said. In general relativity, gravity and matter can trade energy and momentum, with only their combined total conserved. The study shows that reconnection changes the local rate of that exchange.

Reconnection also alters gravitational helicity, the gravitational counterpart of a quantity that measures how twisted and interlinked magnetic field lines are. Frozen-in sheets keep their helicity fixed, but reconnection can create or destroy it.

The findings don't require new physics. "Everything follows from Einstein's general relativity," Comisso said.

"Einstein developed his theory more than a century ago, and it has passed an extraordinary number of experimental tests," he added. "Yet even after more than a century, there are still new insights to be gained from those same equations."

What could trigger gravitational reconnection in nature remains an open question. Among the candidates the researchers suggested are the singularities thought to lurk at the hearts of black holes and the combined effect of gravitational ripples that are too small to track individually. Quantum effects linked to Hawking radiation ‪—‬ the faint glow that black holes are predicted to emit ‪—‬ could also play a part.

"We're still at the beginning, but one of the most interesting possibilities is that gravitational reconnection could play a role in extreme events, such as the merger of two black holes or the collision of neutron stars," Comisso said. "These are environments where gravity is extremely strong and the geometry of spacetime changes dramatically."

Such collisions send out ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, which detectors such as LIGO (the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) have been recording since 2015. "We'd like to understand whether gravitational reconnection could contribute to transferring energy, and whether it might leave a recognizable signature in gravitational waves," Comisso added. "We don't know the answers yet, but these are questions that we can now begin to investigate."

Comisso, L., & Asenjo, F. A. (2026). Reconnection of gravitational fields. Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/lmqy-pf9k

#6409. CT Scans Reveal the Secret of a Mysterious 400-Year-Old Lock

X-ray scans cracked an Elizabethan padlock’s code, revealing how a centuries-old security mechanism worked without damaging an unusually well-preserved piece of maritime history.

For more than 400 years, a brass combination lock recovered from a shipwreck off the Welsh coast kept its secret. Lost when a violent storm wrecked the Ann Francis, the remarkably well-preserved Elizabethan lock still had working letter dials, but no one knew the four-letter combination needed to open it.

Opening it more than 400 years later meant working out its four-letter code without damaging an exceptionally well-preserved Elizabethan artifact, a challenge that brought museum specialists together with researchers more accustomed to studying bones.

The lock came from the Ann Francis, which was returning from Spain when a ferocious storm blew it off course on the evening of December 28, 1583. The ship wrecked on Margam Beach, near Port Talbot, leaving its extraordinary cargo buried beneath the sand for centuries.

Dredging and storms eventually stripped away layers of sand, exposing traces of the sixteenth-century hoard. Metal detectorist Peter Hughes discovered most of it over 21 years, between 1996 and 2017. The finds, recovered by Hughes and other metal detectorists, were subsequently acquired by Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales).

“When I found the lock, I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition. When I moved the ring dials of the combination, they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands, and I was left in disbelief. I also remember being left excited at the prospect of finding wonderful things from the treasure chest it once locked,” said Hughes, finder of the hoard.

What the lock once protected remains uncertain. Researchers believe it secured a small chest containing valuable items, and its position near a collection of Spanish silver coins and two coin weights recovered from the wreck offers some clues. It may have guarded those objects or a chest holding valuables that did not survive, such as documents or textiles.

To investigate the mechanism, museum experts worked with specialists at Cardiff University using micro-CT, a form of X-ray imaging that can reveal fine details inside an object. Dr. David Williams, a postdoctoral research associate based at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility in the university’s School of Engineering, explained the advantage of examining the lock this way.

“Micro-CT scanning allowed us to look inside the lock without damaging it.”

The task was to connect the letters visible on the outside with the concealed parts that determined whether the lock would open. Williams could examine those relationships in the scan, then pass the combination to the museum team for the physical test.

“By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination. We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us. I had to wait until later that evening for the museum team to test the combination, so getting the message that we’d cracked it was incredibly satisfying,” said Williams.

The four letters were ANCE, and when the museum team tested the combination, the centuries-old lock opened.

“It’s not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery!” Williams said.

Its remarkable condition and connection to a shipwreck with a known date make the lock especially valuable as a historical find. Deciphering the combination also leaves a more personal question about whoever chose those letters.

“Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalizing mystery to solve. Of course, now we’ve solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner,” said Alastair Willis, senior curator for numismatics and the Welsh economy at Amgueddfa Cymru.

The lock is currently on display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea alongside other artifacts from the Ann Francis hoard. They include rare gold coins dating from the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain and a boatswain’s whistle recovered from the wreck.

#6407. A 6-Million-Year-Old Whale Had a Face So Strange Scientists Thought It Was Crushed

A newly identified prehistoric whale had unusual adaptations that may have allowed it to hunt along the seafloor millions of years ago.

An ancient whale that lived millions of years ago had a skull so dramatically distorted that its face appeared pushed to one side. Its bony nostrils were displaced entirely to the left, and its oversized snout curved sharply downward. Scientists have identified the animal as Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale with the most extreme facial asymmetry ever documented in a cetacean.

The fossil dates to the Late Miocene, approximately 6.3 to 5.6 million years ago, and belonged to a whale measuring about 2.7 meters (8.9 feet) long. Researchers believe its skull may also represent the greatest facial asymmetry known in any mammal.

Most vertebrates have skulls that are approximately symmetrical, with corresponding structures on either side of the head. Toothed whales are an exception. Their skulls have evolved asymmetrical shapes to accommodate specialized organs involved in producing sound and echolocation, allowing them to navigate and detect prey underwater.

“Cranial asymmetry in toothed whales is directly linked to the development of fatty structures in the forehead that are involved in sound production. But in Scaphokogia huachafo, this asymmetry went far beyond the area around the blowhole. Both bony nostrils are shifted entirely to the left side of the skull, while the facial bones differ dramatically in size and position. The skull looks completely crooked,” explains Aldo Benites-Palomino, lead author of the study. He investigated the fossil during his doctoral research at the University of Zurich and is now an assistant professor at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU).

The whale’s unusual anatomy suggests a feeding strategy very different from that of modern sperm whales, which pursue squid in deep ocean waters. Scaphokogia huachafo appears to have been adapted for searching for food along the bottom of shallow coastal seas. Its thick, tubular snout contained dense bone and hardened cartilage that added weight toward the front of its body. The snout angled downward by 31 degrees, while reconstructions of the joint between the skull and first neck vertebra suggest the animal could lower its head by as much as 55 degrees.

“The entire cranio-cervical complex is modified to point the snout directly toward the bottom,” explains Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, study co-author and doctoral advisor at the University of Zurich. “The combination of dense bone, the downward-curving snout and the flexible neck articulation allowed the animal to move directly above the seabed and feed close to the sediment.”

Unlike some modern marine mammals that forage along the bottom, Scaphokogia lacked specialized facial whiskers and visual adaptations associated with locating prey in sediment. Researchers therefore suspect it relied on its unusually developed biosonar system to detect food hidden in soft seabed deposits. This remains a hypothesis based on its anatomy rather than direct evidence of its hunting behavior. Its specialized ecological niche apparently disappeared as ocean conditions changed near the end of the Miocene.

The skull was recovered in the mid-1990s from the Pisco Formation in southern Peru, a desert region famous for exceptionally preserved marine fossils. Benites-Palomino encountered the specimen in 2015 while working on his bachelor’s thesis at the Museo de Historia Natural in Lima. Its extreme shape initially raised the possibility that geological forces had distorted the skull after the animal died.

“The initial suspicion with skulls this distorted is always taphonomy – that the specimen may have been flattened or twisted by sediment pressure over millions of years,” says Benites-Palomino. “But the sutures are fully closed, and there are no fractures, pathologies or deformations elsewhere on the skull. This was genuine biology, not a result of poor preservation.”

The researchers chose a species name that reflects the animal’s unconventional appearance. Huachafo comes from Peruvian Spanish and describes something extravagant, flashy, bizarre, or aesthetically excessive.

“In Peru, huachafo is an everyday word for anything that is flashy, over-the-top, bizarre, extravagant, or difficult to categorize aesthetically,” says Benites-Palomino.

“When we looked at the proportions of this whale – with its face strongly shifted to the left and its oversized, downward-curving snout – it broke every rule of symmetry and elegance seen in living cetaceans. Its anatomy is so extravagant and odd that huachafo seemed the perfect name for it.”

Reference: “Extreme cranial asymmetry in extinct benthic feeding sperm whales” by Aldo Benites-Palomino, Marcelo R. Sánchez-Villagra, Florencia Paolucci, Jorge Vélez-Juarbe, Alberto Collareta, Apolline Alfsen, Alton Dooley, Dan Omura, Mario Urbina, Rodolfo Salas-Gismondi and Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, 9 November 2026, Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-11074-2

#6406. What’s the Best Snow and Ice Melt? Here’s Why Using Rock Salt Shouldn’t Be Your Default Option.

When you need to keep the driveway ice-free, there’s a wide variety of ice melts to consider.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If the winter weather in recent years hasn’t already been causing some chaos, this year’s Super El Niño isn’t helping. Preparation is key. Setting down a layer of snow and ice melt (i.e., deicers) on your driveway and walkways before a snowstorm hits can save you a lot of time shoveling or snow blowing. But when you walk into the home improvement store, there might be more options than you were prepared for. Don’t worry, with just a little bit of information under your belt, you can choose the best ice melt for the job.

Not all ice melt is created equal. Some melts don’t work as well as others in subzero temperatures and won’t be effective against bonded ice. And some ice melt negatively affects nearby lawns and plants, or causes irritation and health issues for pets. Knowing the difference between the ingredients that power your snow and ice melts is important when choosing the right one for you.

Deicers work by exhibiting one of two thermal reactions: exothermic or endothermic. Exothermic materials, such as sodium chloride and magnesium chloride, release heat when they come into contact with ice or snow. Endothermic materials, such as rock salt and calcium magnesium acetate, absorb heat from their surroundings (such as the sun) and use that heat to melt ice.

Because of this difference, exothermic ice melts perform better in subzero temperatures, and endothermic melts become less effective below 20 degrees Fahrenheit or so, especially at night. However, though exothermic reactions are stronger, they can also be more corrosive and less friendly to plants and animals. Blended melts may offer a good balance, which can help the melt work better in lower temperatures, but also be less corrosive and harmful to pets and plants.

Sometimes referred to as a deicer and often simply called “salt,” ice and snow melts can be made of different chemical compounds or blended to take advantage of their different attributes. This can make some less damaging to pavements or nearby plants. We put together a list of the most typical compounds that you’ll see sold by themselves or in a list of ingredients in blended options, which are the most common types you’ll see at stores.

These are some of the most common types of compounds used for melting ice and snow. Some are sold in their pure form or may be an ingredient in a blended formula.

Exothermic ice melt compounds, such as calcium chloride and magnesium chloride, work better in subzero temperatures because they release heat. If you live in an area where winter temperatures regularly drop below zero, consider one of these types or a blend that contains them.

If your winters are milder and average temperatures tend to hover in the twenties, an endothermic ice melt like rock salt or a urea blend can get the job done. Blended ice melts will often combine exothermic and endothermic compounds to help them perform better in lower temperatures and keep the cost more reasonable. Companies that make these blends will often label the bag with the lowest effective temperature to help you know for sure.

Traditional salts can irritate dog and cat paws, and some of the stronger exothermic compounds that include chlorides can also be irritating or harmful if ingested. The American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) says ingestion can lead to ice melt toxicosis, which can cause vomiting or neurological issues. However, ice melt toxicosis is unlikely to happen from just a few licks; the most serious cause is when a bag of melt is left unattended and ingested by your pet in large amounts.

To help combat this, many brands offer “pet safe” varieties of ice melt, but no blend is truly perfect. These animal-friendly blends tend to eliminate sodium or chloride from the mix, but not all do. The ASPCA recommends using urea-based ice melts, as urea (a compound made of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen) is the least likely ingredient to cause stomach irritation. Another simple idea, especially in cities and suburbs where there is little control over what ice melt the neighbors use, is to adorn your dog in paw booties before taking a walk.

Ice melts that have high concentrations of salts or chlorides can be problematic for vegetation and the environment in general. According to a study by Penn State Extension, when used in large amounts, simple rock salt (sodium chloride) can injure or kill plants near the treated pavement as it washes away, and further pollute waterways, harming fish and other marine life. Instead, the study notes, a compound like calcium magnesium acetate (CMA), which forgoes the use of chlorides or salts, is a safer option for environmentally sensitive areas. Urea-based ice melts are also a good choice.

Like the pet-friendly varieties of deicers, brands can be very loose with how they market their eco-friendly products, especially with the blends; there’s no guarantee that the one you buy won’t partially contain a compound that is harmful in large quantities. If you want to be as eco-friendly as possible, avoid blends that include chlorides and salts.

If that can’t be avoided, just follow the golden rule of “everything in moderation.” After all, overtreating an area is more likely to damage nearby vegetation—even if you use the more environmentally friendly varieties. If you’re still finding noticeable piles of deicer after the snow and ice are gone, you might be using too much.

Corrosion is a considerable problem caused by deicers. Salt-based melts or brines can penetrate porous stone, freeze, and cause the surface to expand. Meanwhile, chlorides can accelerate the rate of corrosion in metal. The Minnesota Pollution Control Agency noted that acetate-based deicers that don’t use chlorides or salts caused low to moderate levels of corrosion, but again, using any ice melt in moderation will help lower the chance of corrosion to your sidewalks, driveways, and nearby railings.

#6405. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

The new Peerium architecture aims to power hyper-efficient computers capable of training AI models with up to 40 trillion parameters.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Engineers in China have built a new computer architecture they say can one day make up to a million artificial intelligence (AI) chips work as one. For comparison, Elon Musk's AI company, SpaceXAI (soon to be SpaceXSI), describes its Colossus cluster as the world's most powerful AI training system, comprising 200,000 interconnected chips.

Traditionally, the AI chips used to train foundation models are housed in separate servers and communicate over a network to share data and divide workloads. But the new architecture, Peerium, uses a high-speed interconnect system designed to maintain efficient communication between chips across multiple racks, even as the number of chips scales into the hundreds of thousands.

Huawei unveiled the new architecture Sept. 17 at the company's annual CONNECT conference.

Representatives from Huawei said in a statement that computers powered by Peerium could train models with up to 40 trillion parameters. For comparison, competing hardware, like GB200 NVL72 from NVIDIA and CS-3 from Cerebras, have reported training at the trillion-parameter scale, rather than the tens-of-trillions.

"Over the next two years, there will be roughly 6 or 7 frontier AI labs in China, and all will aim at training foundation language models of sizes ranging from 10 to 40 trillion parameters," Liao Heng, chief scientist for Huawei's chip design arm HiSilicon, told the Associated Press. "So you need such a scale of infrastructure to train these models."

Peerium's performance relies on three elements: nested parallelism, unified memory addressing, and peer-to-peer interconnects, Huawei representatives said in the statement.

Nested parallelism allows workloads to be broken into smaller tasks and organized across hierarchical groups of chips that work in parallel. It's similar to how a company breaks down work into departments and then smaller teams, all of which coordinate their efforts toward a common goal. Unified memory addressing allows processors to access memory across other servers, as opposed to only that attached to the processor's own server. Peer-to-peer interconnects allow components to communicate more directly with one another, rather than relying on an intermediary.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

All three principles are designed to make more efficient use of computing resources so that a single system can coordinate larger numbers of chips to handle demanding AI workloads.

According to Huawei, existing interconnect technologies — which link processors and servers to enable them to communicate — cannot support the Peerium architecture at the scale it envisages. For instance, NVIDIA uses NVLink for communication within racks and InfiniBand for communication between racks. The inter-rack communication bandwidth in this setup is 200GB per second, Eric Xu, Huawei's rotating chairman, told the AP.

"With such a low inter-rack communications bandwidth, there is no way you can make one million processors work as one computer," he said.

Huawei instead developed its own interconnect technology, UnifiedBus, which the company says delivers inter-rack communications bandwidth of up to 800GB per second.

"When one million processors work as one computer, this lays the foundation for better and more efficient AI training and inference," Xu added. "Therefore, I see UnifiedBus as the path for the future AI era. I believe, in the years to come, other players would certainly follow suit."

Alongside Peerium, Huawei also announced the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, a computing system built on Peerium and powered by more than 8,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT AI accelerator chips.

Xu said testing for AI training is underway on these SuperPoDs and that results show that they use their available computing power for AI training more efficiently than AI computing clusters that aren’t based on Peerium and UnifiedBus.

Huawei expects to begin supplying the SuperPoDs by early next year, at the latest, before its SuperClusters, which link multiple SuperPoDs to form a larger AI computing system, based on Peerium, eventually come online. Representatives said that one SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards — hardware modules that add processing capacity — is currently being deployed and tested.

Models with large numbers of parameters demand greater computing resources and infrastructure, which isn't always desirable as it increases costs. In the summer, researchers used an IBM quantum computer to reduce the perplexity of Meta's Llama 3.1 8B language model — a measure of how well it predicts the next word or token — while keeping the number of parameters almost unchanged.

Fiona Jackson is a freelance writer and editor primarily covering science and technology. She has worked as a reporter on the science desk at MailOnline, and also covered enterprise tech news for TechRepublic, eWEEK, and TechHQ.

Fiona cut her teeth writing human interest stories for global news outlets at the press agency SWNS. She has a Master's degree in Chemistry, an NCTJ Diploma and a cocker spaniel named Sully, who she lives with in Bristol, UK.

#6402. A Lost Landmass Nearly the Size of North America Is Hiding Under the Sea—and It Could Rewrite Human History

A geographer calls it Aquaterra. For 120,000 years, early humans lived there—then the oceans swallowed it.

Several years ago, I travelled to North Carolina as part of a research trip for a story about the famous Lost Colony of Roanoke. Trying to leave no stone unturned, I explored the former colony’s dedicated National Historic Site, poured over archives of antique maps, and even took in a lavish outdoor stage production.

Ultimately, trying to wrangle all the many tendrils of that leviathan proved too unwieldy, and many of the ancillary elements have remained confined to my notebooks. Yet one moment from that trip has never been far from my mind, and it reshaped how I thought about our quest for answers about early human history.

It came about during a conversation with Dr. Eric Klingelhofer, a respected scholar and Vice President for Research with The First Colony Foundation. Dr. Klingelhofer had overseen several excavations that yielded remnants of Roanoke, but he was worried that many once-buried artifacts had already been claimed by a much more powerful force.

“Before my retirement,” he told me, “I attended a UNESCO-backed conference on Bonaire in the Dutch West Indies. These causes, rising sea levels and storm surges, plus coastal overdevelopment, endangered every island, as most prehistoric and early colonial sites lie close to the sea.” As we sat there on tranquil, federally protected land, it was hard for me to feel the urgency at the time, but he stressed that we were in a race against time. “At Fort Raleigh,”—the name the National Parks Service gave the National Historic Site—“coastal erosion has already swallowed up excavation units we had dug in 2007. The rate of loss is about twenty feet in twenty years—and it may be increasing.”

After our conversation, I walked along the island’s shoreline, struck by the thought that although I might be walking the same land as those colonists, the landscape wasn’t really the same. Their shoreline likely sat yards farther out than the one I strolled, and as the water swept that land away, it took with it our chance to learn more about the people who once stood there.

In the study of history, we too often focus on the preservation or replication of what was once on a certain parcel of land, taking it as a given that the land itself stayed constant. We spend all our time debating whether the proverbial Ship of Theseus is still the same after centuries of repairs, never stopping to question if the shoreline of Delos on which he landed still remains.

Yet, recent studies have emerged to remind us that even in the absence of human intervention, the world looked different to the peoples of the past than it does to us today.

The scale of this dilemma, the problem of our submerged history, is far greater than a single island in North Carolina, or a single colony from the 1500s. Our whole understanding of early humankind may be built on faulty ground, due specifically to how much of that ground is now underwater. But don’t let your thoughts drift to that Platonic idea of Atlantis; the proper term, as The Atlantic recently reminded us, is Aquaterra.

In 2014, the geographer Jerome E. Dobson mounted a case for the recognition of a global landmass he dubbed Aquaterra, a term he first proposed in 1999. In “Aquaterra Incognita,” Dobson argued that “all landmasses are defined by time as well as space,” and therefore, since “so little is known about the seacoast where a significant portion of humankind surely dwelled for the better part of 120,000 years,” we should properly recognize and name the 22.5-million-square-kilometer landmass that once hosted the earliest human civilizations.

When we think about the ice ages that have cycled across Earth’s history, we can easily picture the glaciers and ice sheets that formed, but we rarely consider where all that water came from. During an ice age, sea levels drop, exposing land that’s now underwater. As a result, the shorelines early humans knew looked very different from the ones we see today.

The lowlands these glaciers exposed were not bereft of life, either. The ecosystems they once supported varied, from grasslands to wetlands, forests to estuaries. They attracted wildlife, and later, early human civilizations. “Compare the most recent curve of sea level rise against the timeline of cultural innovations,” Dobson writes, “and you will find that much human progress occurred while seacoasts were still quite low.”

When the glaciers melted and sea levels rose again, naturally, early humans abandoned their soon-to-be-submerged settlements. But that doesn’t mean we should simply ignore what once stood there. “It would not change the timeline of human progress if, for instance, cities were found as low as -50 meters, since Jericho is known to have existed when sea levels were that low,” Dobson notes. What could revise that timeline, he notes, is “the possibility that precursors of major innovations may exist at even lower depths.”

“One intriguing possibility is pottery,” he proposes:

All this talk about “possibility,” of course, makes the benefits of recognizing Aquaterra seem entirely theoretical. Yet in just the last few years, the archeological world received a stirring reminder that the land we can see is not the only land there ever was, and that whole chapters of our history may have been claimed by the sea.

In 2021, Michael K. Faught and Morgan F. Smith published “The magnificent seven: Marine submerged precontact sites found by systematic geoarchaeology in the Americas.” The study documented not one or two but seven projects, in North America alone, that had found traces of precontact life now drowned beneath the continental shelf. Each of the seven projects worked “from the terrestrially known, to the submerged unknown.” Using methodical but varied mapping and modeling techniques, researchers predicted where people might once have lived, then searched for proof with underwater surveys, sediment cores, and even hands-on excavations.

One of the research efforts happened in the Gulf of Mexico’s paleo-Sabine River. Over the course of a decade, from 1976 to 1986, it turned up “charred wood and vegetation, nut hulls, seeds, fish scales, and bone from fish, reptiles, birds, and small mammals,” some of which dated back 9,000 years. Soon after, researchers in Belize found the drowned outlines of pole-and-thatch buildings, which turned out to be Classic-period Maya salt works now sitting underwater. Other research discussed in the study uncovered stone tools, campsites, and even a stone artifact more than 12,000 years old.

To truly understand human history, we can’t keep digging only in the land we can see. We also have to search for the land our ancestors knew, much of which now lies beneath the waves. That calls for a change in mindset and a rethinking of how archaeology works. As seas keep rising, how many more once-inhabited places will slip beneath the surface, taking with them secrets as recent as Roanoke’s? If we don’t change course now, the sites we have yet to excavate may be written off by tomorrow’s scholars as mere seafloor.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. As a writer and researcher, he has produced written and audio-visual content for more than fifteen years, spanning historical periods from the dawn of early man to the Golden Age of Hollywood. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.

In this excerpt from "This is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth," author and physicist Christophe Galfard explores the way 19th century scientists were starting to use thermodynamics to understand just how old Earth is.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the 1950s, American geochemist Clair Patterson presented findings that showed Earth is around 4.55 billion years old. His evidence was based on lead isotopic analysis that he used to calculate the age of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, which was discovered in Arizona in 1891. That result is now widely accepted as the age of our planet, but the buildup to this discovery was a long time coming.

Earth's true age was a subject of much debate among scientists in the 19th century. And rather than geologists taking the helm, it was physicists who realized that this giant ball of rock we live on must be far older than the thousands of years that had been assumed in prior centuries. Their main reasoning was heat.

In this excerpt from "This Is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth" (University of Chicago Press/Picador, 2026), author and physicist Christophe Galfard looks at the progression among scientists who were coming to realize that thermodynamics was an essential piece of this long-standing puzzle.

Some two and a half centuries ago, the foremost experts on scientific matters knew a thing or two about heat. They knew, for instance, how heat could be transferred from one place to another. A new science was about to emerge out of this knowledge, a science called thermodynamics, which means "movements of heat" in Greek.

Thermodynamics isn't a force. It is more like a guidebook, a set of rules that apply to large

numbers of particles when they come together. It gives us, humans, a way to understand how particles behave when there is a lot of them without needing to refer to each one of them individually. It shows us how properties that don't exist on their own arise when many particles are together. It deals with these things we call emergent phenomena, such as heat and pressure, and which [Philip] Anderson's "More Is Different" tried to make sense of.

Understanding the dynamics of heat meant a lot to nineteenth-century scientists — so much so that many saw in it the roots of a philosophy so universal and powerful that they thought it should guide us through all our lives. Some even went as far as believing that heat was the source of eternal life. A prominent scientist became so convinced that this was the case that he locked himself up in his house and overheated it, thus shielding himself from all mortal diseases (ageing and death included). The experience was a true torture for the occasional guests who came to visit him, not to mention his wife, who had to endure it day and night.

The scientist held fast to his belief, though, piling on layer after layer of clothing to keep himself ever warmer. Unfortunately, the bulk made it difficult to move, and he eventually missed a step on his own staircase and died from the fall.

As a scientific discipline, thermodynamics was born with a book written in 1824 by a 27-year-old French physicist named Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot, who, as he explained how heat could produce work, told everyone how the steam engine worked.

Lord Kelvin giving a lecture at Glasgow University in 1899.

With Carnot's vision, the way hot objects cool down began to be understood, raising hopes that the resolution of one particular problem might be imminent: the determination of the Earth's age. Were we to somehow guess how hot our planet was at birth, thermodynamics could then be used to tell us how much time had gone by for it to have cooled to its present temperature. Many scientists tried it, keen to be the first one to nail the true age of our world.

Considering our planet in all its complexity to be far too difficult, simplifications were in order, and British physicist William Thomson shot first by picturing our world as a ball. A very simple, rock-solid ball made of pretty much the same stuff throughout, from surface to core. No ocean, no mountain, just a smooth ball the size of the Earth. He then calculated how long it would take it to cool down from being red hot to its present temperature, and declared that the Earth was something between 40 and 400 million years old.

Refining his calculations, he then announced that the world was 100 million years old, before settling for 40 million again.

Thomson's result does not correspond to the true age of the Earth, but it was a start. It was the result of a model, an attempt at figuring out something about our world using still-to-be-refined laws, and mathematical sense. What was more problematic was that no one dared question his results. Even as it shifted from one paper to another, the age of the Earth given by Thomson was always greeted as the right one. A reason for this is that at the end of the nineteenth century Thomson had become Lord Kelvin.

The same Kelvin after whom the Kelvin unit of absolute temperature is named. A scientific superstar who had the power to undo, in a snap of fingers, the career of anyone who disagreed with him.

Lord Kelvin was a physicist, not a geologist, so geologists could have questioned his work, but they didn't. In fact, they weren't bothered. Many of them back then believed that being a geologist was all about intuition and proper English, a language they deemed far more efficient than mathematical gibberish.

That being said, and however wrong the results, Kelvin's calculations were beautiful, giving whoever wanted to think about the problem of the age of the Earth a way forward, which is exactly what one of his former students, Northern Irishman John Perry, did. He thought that Kelvin had overlooked something. As a man of science talking to his former mentor (and job provider), Perry explained his vision to Kelvin but was ignored.

John Perry, a student of Kelvin's, who realized Earth was billions of years old — and that its mantle was a liquid, not a solid.

Still, he published his thoughts in Nature. But again, the article was ignored. Not just by Kelvin, but by the scientific community at large, including geologists.

It would have saved us all quite a bit of time had this not been the case, because Perry not only found a much more correct way to picture the Earth and estimate its age than Kelvin had, but he also found the source of the power that makes our planet's continents drift.

In his model, Perry didn't picture the Earth to be uniformly the same from surface to core as Kelvin had. Instead, he modelled the Earth's interior as being divided into three regions: a metallic core at its centre, a solid crust at its surface, and a mantle that lay in between the two. Rather unexpectedly, Perry didn't envision the mantle as everyone else would have; he believed that it didn't behave like the solid rock it was, but as a liquid.

No wonder his former master didn't take him seriously. However, he pictured the mantle behaving like a liquid only when considered over long periods of time. Sandwiched between a hot core and a colder crust that very much looked like a lid, he believed the mantle had no choice but to behave just like water does in a heated pan, with the hottest parts at the bottom rising and cooling before diving back down and rising up again, in repeated loops, albeit in extremely slow motion. This type of movement is called convection, and it happens in solids, too.

If he was right, there would be two immediate consequences. The first one was that the time it would take for our planet's surface to cool down from red hot to its current temperature could now be far longer than Kelvin had estimated. The lid and the convection patterns prevented our planet from quickly radiating away all its energy into space, so we were now inhabiting an Earth that could be as old as 2 or 3 billion years. Maybe even more. Such timescales were unheard of in the scientific community. Back then, no one knew that the universe itself was 13.8 billion years old. They knew next to nothing.

The second consequence of Perry's model was that the mantle's circular movements underneath the crust could drag the crust itself via friction. The solid surface of our world would then move, and split into pieces that would drift, and collide, and plunge underneath — or slide above — one another. Where they collided, mountain ranges would rise, like the Alps, the Himalayas, the Rockies . . . Where they split apart, rifts would appear, probably in the middle of oceans, along ridges . . . just like [Marie] Tharp had found.

Nowadays, these broken pieces of our planet's surface have all been mapped. They are our world's plates and their movements through time are called plate tectonics. Today, most of us have heard about plate tectonics. Back then, however, no one had, and if very few people remember Perry today, it is because another scientific breakthrough made the estimation of the age of the Earth much easier and precise, showing us that our world isn't 2 or 3 billion years old, as Perry suggested, but precisely 4.567 billion, give or take a few million.

You’ll travel back in time to witness the cataclysmic asteroid impact that doomed the dinosaurs, experience the tumultuous forces that shaped our planet, and discover how the first stirrings of life emerged from inanimate matter.

Christophe Galfard is a theoretical physicist turned international pop-science bestselling author based in Paris. He co-authored "George's Secret Key to the Universe" with Stephen Hawking and his daughter Lucy Hawking. Galfard's most recent book, "The Universe in Your Hand: A Journey Through Space, Time, and Beyond," has been translated into over 20 languages.

#6398. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

A man's appendix had to be removed, but not for dangerous inflammation, as you might expect.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: The man went to the emergency room because he had a sharp pain in his lower-right abdomen.

What happened next: When doctors examined the man, the type of pain and the location of his discomfort suggested that he might have appendicitis, or inflammation of the appendix.

Appendicitis can be dangerous because it can cause the appendix to burst and release bacteria from the bowels into the abdominal cavity, thereby infecting the cavity's lining. This infection, called peritonitis, can spread to the bloodstream and cause the life-threatening condition sepsis, which kicks the immune system into overdrive.

Even though the patient had acute pain in his lower-right abdomen, he did not show signs of peritonitis, such as fever, nausea, symptoms of dehydration and an elevated heart rate, according to a report of his case. His doctors then performed abdominal ultrasound scans and found that the man's abdominal organs, including the appendix, appeared normal, with no signs of inflammation.

The report's authors did not include details about the man's treatment after this examination. But eight months later, he was still in pain and returned to the hospital for further evaluation, they noted.

The diagnosis: This time, when medical personnel questioned the man, he recalled that approximately 15 years earlier, he had accidentally swallowed a piece of a long bone containing edible marrow. The report does not mention if the man sought treatment immediately after swallowing this bone.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

At this second visit, doctors performed an abdominal X-ray and found a round object near the upper right of the man's pelvis. It measured about an inch (2.5 centimeters) long and a little over an inch (3 cm) wide.

According to a subsequent CT scan, the object contained bone tissue and was near the appendix. When the doctors looked inside the patient's abdomen with a laparoscope — a long, flexible tool with a camera at one end — they saw that the appendix was enlarged.

The treatment: Surgeons performed a laparoscopic appendectomy, which uses small incisions in the abdomen to insert instruments for removing the appendix. Inside the appendix was a hardened mass of fecal matter, called a fecaloma, which surrounded a long bone.

The organ's muscular walls had been stretched out by the mass, but there were no signs of inflammation. No complications developed after the surgery, and the patient was discharged two days later. The report does not describe any follow-up visits or treatments.

The appendix (orange) is a small, thin pouch of tissue attached to the colon.

What makes the case unique: It's relatively uncommon for people to accidentally swallow something indigestible and then require a medical visit for it. In the United States annually, about 120,000 people — roughly 90% of whom are children — are treated for ingesting foreign objects, and most of the objects are swallowed accidentally. Most commonly, the adults requiring treatment have ingested jewelry, while children are more likely to swallow coins, toys and batteries.

Typically, small, swallowed items pass harmlessly through the intestines within 48 hours; less than 1% require surgical intervention. Some objects, however, need immediate attention. For example, sharp items can tear the esophagus or puncture digestive organs. Batteries are hazardous if swallowed, as they contain corrosive acid that can leak into the gut. And small magnets are a big risk, especially if two or more are involved, since they may stick together through intestinal walls, which can tear holes in tissues or cause blockages and contortions in the intestines.

Swallowed foreign bodies rarely affect the appendix. Whether they enter the organ depends on the size of the opening into the appendix where it connects to the colon (which can vary between individuals), the dimensions of the ingested object, and the appendix's position in the body at the time. These objects cause approximately 0.005% cases of appendicitis, according to the man's case report. Such items recovered by surgeons through appendectomies include pieces of coal, nails, bits of enamel and glass, shells, dental crowns and bullets.

When a foreign body migrates to the appendix, it typically generates appendicitis within a few months, at most. However, this is not always the case. One report described a man who had eaten pigeons as a child and discovered more than 30 years later that he had 27 lead shot pellets in his appendix. Despite containing these pellets from the birds' flesh, his appendix was not inflamed.

"It is therefore possible, although rare, that a foreign body in the appendix even after many years (in our case, 15 years) does not lead to an authentic appendicitis either histologically or clinically," the authors of the marrowbone case report wrote.

They added that their patient was the first record in the scientific literature of a sizable bone lingering inside an appendix for more than a decade without causing significant inflammation. His pain was likely caused by physical shifting of the hard mass. His experience presented "a unique clinical picture," the doctors wrote.

"This case could offer a possible diagnostic and therapeutic option for appropriately treating patients with foreign bodies within the appendix," they said.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

#6393. AI Surveillance Could Be Harming Your Health. Here’s How.

Doctors from Harvard and Johns Hopkins warn that mass surveillance is a health hazard—and AI is making it much worse.

When CEOs and scientists wax poetic about the potential benefits of AI, the technology’s impact on human health often rises to the top—and in many ways, they’re not wrong. Artificial intelligence’s ability to sift through massive datasets makes these algorithms ideal for spotting early-stage cancer or discovering novel drugs. The United Nations even notes that AI-powered disease surveillance could detect potential outbreaks quickly and prevent crises from spiraling into global pandemics.

However, like any tool, artificial intelligence can also be used for nefarious purposes, and a new perspective published in the New England Journal of Medicine highlights a particularly insidious one and its potential impacts on human health: mass surveillance. Debates over how governments and companies collect our personal data are usually framed as civil liberties or national security issues. But experts from Massachusetts General Hospital, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, and Harvard Medical School say that being watched can make us sick, and in the age of AI, things could get much, much worse.

The authors identify at least three ways surveillance harms health. First, knowing (or even believing) that you’re constantly being monitored can lead to hypervigilance and chronic “anticipatory stress,” which takes a toll on both physical and mental health. Second, surveillance can scare vulnerable people away from essential health behaviors. This includes groups with a reasonable fear of persecution, such as undocumented immigrants or people seeking reproductive or gender-affirming care, who may avoid pharmacies and clinics, hold back details from their doctors, or even skip buying groceries. Third, surveillance data can be used to hand out things that shape our health, like insurance, housing, and jobs, unequally.

“Historically, mass surveillance programs in the United States have most often been organized by government agencies and subject to democratic oversight,” the authors write. “AI-enabled surveillance, however, relies on data ecosystems that are controlled primarily by private companies.”

That’s a big distinction. The Fourth Amendment’s protections are limited when people voluntarily share information with third parties, even if they don’t realize they’re doing so. HIPAA also generally doesn’t cover data collected by consumer-facing tech companies. As a result, AI companies and other private actors can access and analyze vast amounts of personal data, and they could share it with the government without your knowledge or permission. Traditional surveillance usually needed human oversight. AI, by contrast, can continuously comb through social media, search results, financial transactions, geolocation records, and camera footage, then combine it all into increasingly powerful predictions.

This concern isn’t without real-world precedent. The Denver-based Palantir Technologies, founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, developed AI-enabled tools for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), including a system known as ImmigrationOS. ICE has used these tools to combine information from multiple government databases, including visa histories and Medicaid records, to target people for immigration enforcement. Another tool, called Enhanced Leads Identification and Targeting for Enforcement (ELITE), pulls names, photos, addresses, and race and ethnicity data from Medicaid records to map areas with people who could be detained, according to reporting in The BMJ. It can reportedly even generate a “confidence score” for whether someone might be at home.

For the authors, all this surveillance amounts to a public health problem. When data collected for health care or social services can be repurposed for surveillance, trust erodes, and people may stop using vital programs. That’s why they argue that AI-enabled mass surveillance should be considered an emerging “structural determinant of health,” which they define as a social, political, environmental, or economic condition that shapes how health and illness are distributed across a population.

“We believe medicine has an urgent responsibility to confront these developments,” the authors write. “Decisions about AI-enabled mass surveillance are being made with limited input from health experts, even though these systems have clear consequences for population health.” Health care technologies can contribute to the problem, too. Clinicians increasingly recommend wearables and smartphone apps that continuously collect patient data, which means the medical system may be feeding the same data streams that could be used for surveillance.

The courts offer another option. More than 20 state attorneys general have sued the federal government for sharing Medicaid data with ICE and Palantir, and the authors say health care institutions can support these lawsuits by publicly opposing troubling data-sharing deals. Clinicians can also help by documenting patients’ fears about how their data is used and any resulting changes in whether they seek care, which gives litigators and policymakers evidence to work with.

AI surveillance could still be a boon to public health. The same ability to rapidly pull together data from different sources that makes it dangerous could also help health officials spot and respond to threats more effectively. In the end, AI is just a tool, and it’s up to us how we use it. But the authors warn that we may not have long to decide. By the time AI surveillance’s effects become fully apparent, its infrastructure “may already be deeply embedded in everyday life.” As they put it, “The norms established today could determine whether AI-enabled surveillance becomes a tool in service to population health or a driver of avoidable health inequities and structural harm.”

#6392. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.
